output: This review looked at 49 studies involving 3639 people who had diabetes-related nerve problems. These studies mostly came from China and tested different herbal medicines. Some studies said the herbal medicines helped improve symptoms like pain or numbness, but the results weren't very strong because the studies weren't done very well. Not enough information was given about any bad side effects from the medicines. In some studies, the medicines seemed to help, but in others, the bad side effects happened in the group taking the medicine. Because the studies weren't done well, we can't be sure if the herbal medicines are safe or effective. Overall, there's no good evidence that these herbal medicines work better than usual care for nerve problems in people with diabetes. We need more studies to know if they're safe and if they really help.

output: This review looked at five studies involving 1503 women. The studies compared different birth control methods: combined oral contraceptives (COCs), transdermal patches, vaginal rings, and two types of intrauterine devices (IUDs). The studies didn't find a big difference in how well these methods worked or how often people stopped using them. Some studies had small numbers of women. One study found that fewer women stopped using COCs because of personal reasons compared to those using the LNG-IUS 20. Another study showed that the LNG-IUS 12 and LNG-IUS 16 worked about the same over time. In three studies, the LNG-IUS continued to work well for at least 6 to 36 months. The evidence isn't strong enough to say which method works best for young women. More studies are needed to compare these methods.

output: Three small studies looked at using a treatment called CSFD to help prevent damage to the spine after certain types of major abdominal surgeries. In one study, 30% of people who got CSFD had problems with their legs compared to 33% of those who didn't get it. This wasn't a big difference. Another study found that using CSFD along with another medicine helped reduce the number of people who had leg problems after surgery. But this study was too small to be sure. The third study found that 12.2% of people who didn't get CSFD had problems with their legs, compared to only 2.7% of those who did get it. This means CSFD might help prevent leg problems after surgery. When we put all the studies together, CSFD seems to reduce the chance of leg problems by about half. However, there isn't enough information yet to know if CSFD really helps or not. More studies are needed to find out.

output: This review looked at studies comparing ibuprofen to a sugar pill or other medicines for treating migraine headaches. It found that ibuprofen works better than a sugar pill in reducing headache pain and making you feel better after two hours. The higher dose of ibuprofen (400 mg) was better at relieving headache pain within two hours compared to a lower dose (200 mg). Soluble forms of ibuprofen (which dissolve quickly in the mouth) worked better than regular tablets for quick relief. However, ibuprofen didn't work any better than another medicine called rofecoxib for longer-lasting relief. Most people who took ibuprofen had only mild side effects, like feeling sick or dizzy, which went away quickly. Overall, ibuprofen helps about half of people with migraines feel better, but it doesn't completely stop the pain or other symptoms for most people. More studies are needed to confirm these findings.

output: Nine studies looked at feeding preterm babies who are learning to eat normally after being fed through a tube. These studies were not perfect and had some problems like not being able to hide who was getting which food. When comparing responsive feeding (where the baby decides when to eat) to scheduled feeding (where the baby eats at set times), the studies suggested that responsive feeding might help babies start eating solids faster and gain weight more slowly. However, the evidence isn't very strong because the studies weren't well done. It's not clear if this helps babies stay in the hospital longer. The studies didn't ask parents or caregivers about their experiences. So, we don't have strong proof that responsive feeding changes important things for preterm babies or their families. Some studies show that babies who feed when they're hungry might start eating solid foods sooner. But we need more research to know if this is true and if it affects other important things.

output: This review looked at 45 studies comparing Patient Education Materials (PEMs) to no intervention. Most of the studies (44 out of 45) compared PEMs to nothing. One study compared a paper version to a digital version. When PEMs were compared to no intervention, they seemed to improve how healthcare providers do their jobs, though the improvement was small. Some studies showed that patients also benefited, but not all studies looked at patient outcomes. The review found that PEMs helped professionals do their jobs better, but it's not clear if this helps patients. We don't know which features of PEMs make them work best. While PEMs might help a little bit, we don't have enough information to say if they're better than other ways of teaching or if they work well when used with other things. More research is needed to find out.

output: This review looked at five studies with a total of 734 people to see if VGB or CBZ helped treat epilepsy better. Only one study was done well enough to count. The other four were not very good. It was hard to combine the results from all the studies because they didn't measure everything the same way. VGB didn't seem to help people stop taking their medicine sooner or get better faster than CBZ. But VGB caused more people to gain weight and fewer to have skin rashes or feel sleepy. There wasn't much information about problems with eyesight. Right now, we don't know if VGB is better or worse than CBZ for treating epilepsy. Since many people who take VGB lose their eyesight, doctors should use it carefully and check eyesight often. More research is needed to understand why eyesight problems happen and how to prevent them. Future studies should follow rules set by experts and make sure they are done well.

output: This review looked at 41 studies involving 200 healthcare practices and over 48,000 patients. Most studies were not very well done, but they all tried to help people with diabetes in different ways. Some studies focused on doctors and nurses, others on the whole hospital, and some did both. Many studies added teaching patients about their condition. Studies that used multiple methods like training doctors and nurses, improving hospital routines, and giving patients more education showed better results in how well diabetes was managed. Adding patient education or having nurses help patients stick to their treatment plans seemed to help patients feel better too. So, using different strategies to train doctors and nurses, make sure patients get regular check-ups, and teach patients about their condition can help manage diabetes better.

output: This review looked at fifteen studies involving 687 people. The studies were not very good and often had small numbers of participants. Some studies showed that relaxation therapy might help reduce the need for quick-relief medicines, but the results weren't always clear. Relaxation therapy didn't seem to improve lung function tests (FEV1) in most cases. It did seem to improve quality of life for some people. Biofeedback therapy helped with peak flow rates, but relaxation therapy didn't. Relaxation therapy didn't seem to help with depression. The results were mixed because different types of therapies were used. Overall, there isn't enough strong evidence to say if these psychological treatments work for asthma. We need bigger, better-designed studies to find out if these methods are helpful for treating asthma in adults.

output: This study looked at 135 women with mild pre-eclampsia near the end of their pregnancy. The study compared magnesium sulphate, a medicine often used to help prevent seizures, with a placebo (a sugar pill). The study found that magnesium sulphate did not improve the baby's Apgar score, which measures how well the baby is doing right after birth. It also did not affect how early the baby was born. However, more women in the magnesium sulphate group had side effects like feeling warm and flushed. There were no serious side effects that stopped treatment. The study did not find any differences in other problems like bleeding after birth or having a cesarean section. While the study didn't show that magnesium sulphate helps the baby's brain, more research is needed to see if it might help babies born at full term. Also, ways to make the medicine less likely to cause side effects in mothers need to be studied further.

output: This review looked at different dressings and topical agents used for healing wounds after surgery. One small study suggested that aloe vera might slow down healing, but the results aren't clear because some people didn't finish the study. Using a special plaster cast instead of elastic bandages helped wounds heal faster. Other dressings like gauze, foam, and alginate didn’t seem to make much difference in how quickly wounds healed. Gauze caused more pain for patients compared to other dressings. Patients were less happy with gauze dressings too. Gauze is cheaper but it takes more nurse time to care for it. Some studies showed no difference in how long people stayed in the hospital. But one study found that using a plaster cast instead of elastic bandages after an amputation might make people stay in the hospital for fewer days. Overall, the evidence isn’t strong enough to know if different dressings help wounds heal better. Foam seems to be a good choice instead of gauze, as it causes less pain and makes patients happier.

output: This review looked at 16 studies, but only 3 met the criteria to include in the analysis. These studies involved 212 people with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). Most of the studies followed good methods, but the results weren't strong enough to show that exercise therapy helps with things like how well someone can do daily activities, their quality of life, or how well their lungs work. The studies didn't find any harmful side effects from exercise. Based on the information we have, it seems that exercise therapy might help a little bit, but the evidence isn't strong enough to say for sure. There aren't many studies, so we can't be confident that exercise works for everyone. All the studies agreed that exercise doesn't make arthritis worse. To better understand if exercise helps, we need to use the same way to measure how well people are doing after exercise in all studies. While exercise looks promising in the short term, we don't know yet if it helps in the long run.

output: This review looked at four studies with a total of 3090 people who had sudden cardiac arrest. Some studies were done better than others. When comparing two ways to treat sudden cardiac arrest, one way involved doing CPR for a bit longer before using a shock, and the other involved giving a shock right away. The studies didn't show a clear difference in how many people survived to go home from the hospital or how many had good brain function after they came back to life. Both ways of treating sudden cardiac arrest seemed to work about the same. The studies weren't perfect, so we can't be sure which way is better. More research is needed with bigger studies to figure out if one way works better than the other.

output: Four studies with 125 participants looked at whether pulsed electromagnetic fields or capacitive coupled electric fields help treat broken bones that haven't healed properly. While all the studies tried to keep things fair by making sure neither the doctors nor the patients knew who got the treatment or the placebo, each study had some problems. The studies found that the treatment didn't seem to make broken bones heal faster than usual. There was a lot of difference between the studies, which made it hard to know if the treatment really works. The studies didn't find that the treatment helped with pain or made it easier for people to move around. One study had a few small problems. Based on this limited information, we can't say for sure if these treatments work better than usual care. We need more studies to learn more about whether these treatments might help.

At 3 to 6 months, there wasn't enough information to know if doing exercises helped people live longer or if it caused more serious problems. At 12 months, we don't know if exercising helped people go back to work. We need better studies to see if exercising helps people after heart valve surgery, especially in terms of living longer or feeling better.

output: This review looked at 26 studies involving 2066 patients to see if silver dressings helped heal wounds better than regular dressings. For burns, one study found that using silver nitrate was better at preventing infections, but three studies showed that silver sulphadiazine cream caused more infections. Another study found that a special silver dressing called Hydron AgSD was better at preventing infections than silver sulphadiazine cream. For other types of wounds, most studies didn't find a difference in how well silver dressings worked compared to regular ones. One study found that a silver-coated gauze was better at preventing infections, but another found that silver sulphadiazine cream caused more infections. Only one study found that a silver-containing dressing helped wounds heal faster in people with diabetes. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say if silver dressings help wounds heal or prevent infections. Some studies suggest that silver dressings might not be as good as regular ones.

output: Two studies looked at different ways to help manage health care in districts. One study in Cambodia found that using private contracts with international non-governmental organizations (NGOs) to run health systems can make it easier for people to get health care, like antenatal care and using public health centers. This happened because more people started using these services. However, the study didn't find that these contracts helped improve overall health in the area. Another study found that giving managers training every few months can help them do their jobs better. But, this study only looked at three countries in Latin America. We know that these methods can work, but we need more studies to be sure they work everywhere. There are other ideas, like making rules by the government or offering support programs, that might also help, but we haven't studied those enough yet.

output: This review looked at five studies comparing different treatments after surgery and radiation therapy for women with certain types of cancer. The studies found that adding chemotherapy to the treatment after surgery helped keep the cancer from coming back and reduced the chance of dying. When newer types of chemotherapy drugs called platinum-based drugs were used, the chances of living longer were even better. Adding chemotherapy to the treatment after surgery didn't seem to help prevent the cancer from spreading outside the pelvis, but it might still be useful when used with radiation therapy. Overall, chemotherapy seems to be helpful in keeping the cancer from coming back and reducing the risk of dying, especially when used with newer chemotherapy drugs.

output: The review looked at six trials that mostly involved preterm babies. Four small trials found that giving cysteine, a type of amino acid, along with their regular feedings didn't help their growth. But one big study found that giving cysteine helped keep the babies' bodies from losing too much protein (nitrogen retention) in their pee. Cysteine also made the babies' blood have more cysteine, which is good. However, the big study didn't find that cysteine helped prevent serious problems like breathing trouble, eye damage, or gut issues. The review suggests that giving cysteine to preterm babies might help them keep more protein in their bodies. But it's not clear if cysteine causes any bad side effects, like making the baby's pee more acidic. The big study also found no clear benefits from giving another form of cysteine called N-acetylcysteine to very tiny preemies. More research is needed to know if N-acetylcysteine helps or causes any problems.

output: The review looked at six trials with 1758 participants who had mild to moderate heartburn. Most participants were younger adults, but one group was older adults. The trials compared taking proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) as needed (on-demand) versus every day (continuous). Taking PPIs as needed might make it harder to keep your heartburn away (less 'symptom control'), but it can also reduce how many pills you take each week (less 'drug burden'). People might also feel less satisfied with taking PPIs as needed. The trials didn't look at costs or if stopping the medicine caused any good changes. For people with mild heartburn, using PPIs as needed might cause more stomach upset (like feeling full or getting acid in your throat) but might help you take fewer pills. But we don't know if stopping the medicine has long-term benefits or harms because the studies weren't designed to find out.

output: The review looked at 39 studies to see if using a urinary catheter after surgery helps prevent urinary tract infections. Some studies showed that using a catheter might lead to more people needing another catheter, but it wasn't clear if this caused more infections. Other studies suggested that removing the catheter sooner might help prevent infections. However, the studies were small and not always done well, so it's hard to know for sure which method works best. The decision often depends on balancing the risk of getting an infection against the risk of needing another catheter. More research is needed to make a clearer recommendation.

output: This review looked at 75 studies with 7957 people who have irritable bowel syndrome. Some studies were done well, but most weren't. Different herbs were tested to see if they helped. Several herbs, like a Chinese formula, individualized Chinese herbs, and others, seemed to help overall symptoms more than a sugar pill. When compared to regular medicine, about half of the herbs tested helped more. Combining some herbs with regular medicine seemed to work better than just using regular medicine alone. No serious side effects were found. While some herbs might help, the studies weren't always done well. We need more high-quality studies to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at 21 studies involving over 17,000 women and their babies. Most of the studies were done well and had low risk of bias. Women who took zinc during pregnancy had a small chance of having a baby born too early, compared to those who didn't take zinc. However, zinc didn't seem to help with babies being born too small. Zinc didn't show any clear benefits for other health outcomes like stillbirth or newborn deaths. The evidence for zinc helping prevent preterm births is good, but it mainly comes from studies in poorer areas. The evidence isn't strong enough to say zinc helps with other important outcomes. It's important to focus on improving overall nutrition for pregnant women in poor areas, rather than just giving them zinc supplements.

output: This review looked at one new study added to the previous ones. It included 11 trials with 753 participants. The results show that giving extra oxygen to women having a baby through a cut in the tummy (caesarean section) do not seem to make a big difference in how well their babies start breathing right after birth (Apgar scores). The studies also found that women who got extra oxygen had better oxygen levels in their blood, which means they had more oxygen. However, the evidence is not very strong because it comes from studies that might have some flaws. So, while the extra oxygen didn't seem to help the babies breathe better, it did seem to give the mothers and babies a bit more oxygen in their blood. More research is needed to be sure about these findings.

output: This review looked at 23 studies that tested different ways to teach young women about sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and safer sex practices. Most of these studies happened in the United States and were done in health clinics. The studies varied in how long they lasted, how much time people spent learning, who gave the information, and what they focused on teaching. Some covered HIV, chlamydia, and other STIs, but not HPV or cervical cancer. Many of the studies found that teaching young women about STIs helped them use condoms more often. But it didn't always work to get them to stop having sex or have less sex. The studies weren't perfect, so we're not sure how well they worked. It's important to continue studying these methods, especially focusing on HPV and how it can lead to cervical cancer. Future studies should try to answer more questions and see if these methods really help in the long run. They should also look at costs and whether these programs are worth doing. It would be helpful to do more studies in other countries too.

output: This review looked at three studies involving 148 premature babies to see if midazolam, a medicine used to help calm them, worked better than a sugar drink. The studies showed that babies given midazolam were calmer, but it might take them longer to leave the special baby hospital. Some studies found that babies given midazolam had fewer pain signals, but another study suggested they might have more brain problems later. The studies weren't perfect, so we're not sure if midazolam is safe or helpful for these tiny babies. More research is needed to know if midazolam is good or bad for premature babies.

output: This review looked at 582 records and found 10 more by searching other places. After removing duplicates and checking titles and abstracts, we ended up with 17 full papers to look at closely. Out of these, 15 were not about preventing SUDEP, so we didn't include them. One study was still unsure if it fit. The only study we could fully look at suggested that having someone watch over you during sleep might help prevent something called SUDEP, which is a rare but dangerous problem for people who have seizures. This study found that having someone supervise during sleep seemed to lower the chance of SUDEP. But the evidence isn't very strong because the study wasn't perfect. output: The review looked at 15 studies involving 1022 adults with wrist fractures that were out of place. Most studies compared how well external fixation (a type of surgery) worked compared to using a plaster cast. While external fixation kept the fractures in better position and helped prevent problems later, it also led to more complications like infections. The studies weren't perfect because they didn't always do things the same way. Overall, there isn't strong enough evidence to say external fixation leads to better long-term recovery. However, it seems to work better at keeping the bones in good shape right after surgery. More research is needed to know if it's better for overall recovery.

output: This review looked at 13 studies with 1158 people to see if naltrexone worked better than other treatments for people trying to stop using opioids, like drugs like heroin. When comparing naltrexone to a sugar pill or no medicine, it didn't seem to help much. But when people were forced to take their medicine, naltrexone seemed to keep more people in treatment. It didn't work better than talk therapy or other medicines like benzodiazepines or buprenorphine. The studies weren't big enough to show if naltrexone really helps or not. So right now, we don't have enough good evidence to say that naltrexone is better than other treatments for people trying to stop using opioids. More studies are needed to know if it works well.

output: This review looked at 37 trials with 9312 patients. It found that combining radiation therapy (RT) with chemotherapy (CRT) was better than RT alone for overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). CRT was also better than chemotherapy alone (CT) for PFS. However, CRT was linked to more side effects like secondary tumors (SM) compared to CT, especially in advanced stages. For early-stage disease, CRT was better at preventing the cancer from coming back (smoothing recurrence). But for advanced stages, CT alone might cause fewer side effects. Combining RT with chemotherapy (EF-RT) was better at stopping the cancer from getting worse or coming back (PFS) than using RT alone (IF-RT), but it didn't seem to affect overall survival. Overall, CRT seems to be the best choice for early-stage disease, but CT might be better for advanced stages. More recent and detailed studies would help us understand these results better.

output: This study looked at 40 infants and 42 women who were part of a trial comparing two ways to deliver babies with a condition called gastroschisis. The trial wasn't big enough to show if one way was better than the other. Babies born early (at 36 weeks instead of full term) didn't seem to have better or worse outcomes. They didn't live longer or weigh more. They didn't need more help breathing or get sick. The trial couldn't tell us if one way was better for mommies either. The main reason for the difference in when the babies were born might be that some moms naturally went into labor earlier. Because the study was small and not designed to look at these things, we can't say for sure if one way is better or worse. More research is needed to find out.

output: This review looked at studies comparing two medicines, amantadine and rimantadine, to treat and prevent influenza A in children and older adults. Amantadine was found to be effective in preventing influenza A in children, reducing the risk from 10 out of every 100 to 1 out of every 100. However, the evidence is considered low quality, and the safety of these drugs is not well understood. Rimantadine helped reduce fever in children who had the flu, but it didn't help prevent the flu in older adults. The evidence for rimantadine in older adults is very low quality. There were no serious side effects from taking these medicines. Overall, the evidence doesn't strongly support using amantadine or rimantadine to prevent, treat, or shorten the flu in children or older adults. More research is needed.

output: This review looked at 88 trials that tested different ways to help people with allergies. Most of the trials didn't do a good job hiding who got which treatment, which might have made the results less reliable. Overall, the trials showed that immunotherapy (a type of treatment that helps the body get used to allergens) helped reduce asthma symptoms and the need for medicine. It also helped make the airways less sensitive to allergens. However, it didn't seem to improve lung function much. About one out of every five people who tried immunotherapy had a small reaction, like swelling or hives. And about one out of every ten had a bigger reaction that could be more serious. While immunotherapy helped with asthma symptoms and the need for medicine, it's not clear if the benefits are as big as using inhaled steroids, which are another common treatment. More research is needed to confirm these findings and to better understand the risks.

output: This study looked at 38 women who were pregnant and had a condition called immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), which means their blood doesn't have enough platelets. The study gave some women a medicine called betamethasone and others didn't get it. It found that betamethasone did not help prevent babies from having too few platelets or bleeding more than usual. The study did not look at other serious problems like the mother dying or the baby dying. Based on this study, we don't know if betamethasone helps treat ITP in pregnant women. We also don't know if other medicines work better. More studies are needed to find out if any medicine is helpful for ITP during pregnancy. Until we have better information, doctors shouldn't usually give betamethasone to pregnant women with ITP. Future studies should look at many different possible problems to see if any medicine might be good for ITP during pregnancy.

output:
This review looked at different ways to help people with chronic pain feel better. It found that Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), which helps people think differently about their pain, can make some people feel less sad and worried about their pain right after the therapy ends. But these changes don't last very long. CBT also helped people do more activities and feel less scared about their pain. 

When compared to regular care, CBT seemed to help people with pain feel better right away, but the benefits didn't last. Behavior therapy, which teaches people different ways to handle their pain, didn't seem to help much. 

CBT worked best for making people feel less scared about their pain and for helping them do more activities. But it didn't always help with pain itself or make people feel less sad. 

More research is needed to figure out exactly what parts of CBT work best for different people and why. Right now, we don't need more big studies comparing CBT to other treatments, but we do need smaller studies that look at different parts of CBT and how they affect different people.

output: This review looked at 26 studies with 4893 participants who took different types of pain medicines called opioids. Most people stopped taking these medicines because they caused side effects like feeling sick or their pain wasn't relieved well enough. Only a tiny number of people developed a problem with becoming addicted to the medicine. Opioids helped reduce pain, but how much it helped varied from study to study. The studies didn't have enough information to show if taking opioids made people's lives better or if they could do more things. Some people stop taking opioids because of side effects or not getting enough pain relief. But the weak evidence suggests that people who keep taking opioids still feel less pain. It's hard to tell if taking opioids makes people's lives better or worse. Common side effects include feeling sick or having headaches, but serious problems like addiction are rare.

output: This review looked at 30 studies with 4344 people who took different medicines for seasonal allergies affecting their eyes. The studies compared medicines like olopatadine, ketotifen, and others. Most studies compared olopatadine to a placebo (a pretend medicine). The studies lasted from one to eight weeks. Only one study could be fully analyzed. The results show that using medicines like olopatadine or ketotifen can help reduce allergy symptoms in the short term, compared to using nothing. However, there isn't enough information about how long these medicines work or if they work better than each other. Also, the studies didn't always report the same things, making it hard to compare them directly. Overall, these medicines seem safe and don't cause serious side effects. More studies are needed to know if they work longer and if one is better than another.

output:
This review looked at four studies that lasted from 24 to 52 weeks and involved 2250 people who were randomly assigned to use either insulin detemir or glargine. Most of the studies had some problems in how they were done, so we can't be completely sure about their results. Insulin glargine was taken once a day in the evening, while insulin detemir could be taken once a day or twice a day depending on the study. At the end of the studies, people using insulin detemir were taking it twice a day in a higher dose compared to those using glargine. 

Both insulins helped keep blood sugar levels under control, but there wasn't much difference between them. Neither insulin caused more nighttime or severe low blood sugar levels. Insulin detemir led to less weight gain. People using insulin glargine needed to take less insulin each day and had fewer skin reactions where they injected the insulin. 

There wasn't enough information to tell if one insulin was better for quality of life or cost. Only one study looked at how well people felt overall, and it didn't show any big differences between the two insulins. Overall, the review suggests that there isn't a clear difference in how well insulin detemir and insulin glargine work for controlling blood sugar levels.

output:
Three trials involving 6343 participants looked at whether removing blockages in the neck arteries (carotid endarterectomy) helps prevent strokes. When we carefully reviewed the data from all three trials, we found that:

- Removing blockages didn't help prevent strokes in people with very mild blockages.
- It helped a little bit in people with moderate blockages.
- It helped a lot in people with severe blockages that weren't completely blocked.
- It didn't seem to help in people whose arteries were almost completely blocked.

The results show that removing blockages in the neck arteries might help prevent strokes, especially in people with severe blockages that aren't completely blocked. However, it doesn't seem to help in people whose arteries are almost completely blocked. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at 12 studies with 1023 participants comparing different types of dressings for treating venous leg ulcers. The studies didn't find a clear difference in how well these dressings helped wounds heal compared to each other. Some dressings like hydrocellular foam and hydrocolloid dressings didn't show better healing than others like polyurethane foam, paraffin gauze, hydrocapillary dressing, knitted viscose dressing, or protease modulating matrix. Also, there wasn't much difference in how often people had bad reactions to the dressings. Most of the studies had some problems that might have affected their results. Based on this limited information, we can't say for sure that any type of dressing works better than others for healing these ulcers. The evidence isn't very strong because it's based on a few studies that weren't perfect. We need more good studies to know if foam dressings are helpful or not.

output: This review looked at six studies involving 1,124,483 newborns, focusing on cystic fibrosis (CF). One study was large enough to include in the analysis. The study found that babies who were screened for CF were less likely to have severe malnutrition compared to those who weren't screened. Specifically, fewer screened babies were below the 10th percentile for weight and height. By age 7, more screened babies had lung function within normal limits. At the time of diagnosis, screened babies had better chest X-ray scores. However, over time, chest X-ray scores got worse in the screened group. The study suggests that screening might be less expensive than traditional diagnosis. Screening appears to help with lung health early on, but it's not clear if it leads to better long-term outcomes because other factors can affect how well people with CF do.

output: This review looked at four studies that tested different ways to help people stop smoking. Two studies used medicine along with talking therapies, and two used just talking therapies. When all the studies were put together, it showed that the therapies helped people stop smoking better than just taking medicine. But when only the best studies were looked at, the result wasn't as clear. The review found that Indigenous people have more problems from smoking than others. There isn't much information about helping Indigenous people stop smoking. The few studies that did look at this showed that talking therapies can help Indigenous people stop smoking too. But the evidence isn't strong because there aren't many good studies. More research is needed to help reduce health problems from smoking among Indigenous people.

output: This review looked at five studies involving 247 babies to see if letting them sleep in a special bed called a cot instead of an incubator helped keep their body temperature normal. The studies didn't show a big difference in body temperature between the two methods. However, more babies in the cot group had higher temperatures sometimes. Babies who slept in the cot were less likely to be breastfed and less likely to survive until they left the hospital. Using a heated water-filled mattress in the cot method didn't help with weight gain in the first week, but it didn't hurt either. Overall, the results suggest that letting babies sleep in a cot isn't better than using an incubator for keeping their temperature normal or helping them grow. More research is needed to know if this is true in different places, especially in countries where resources might be limited.

output: Four studies with 1485 participants who had moderate to severe Crohn's disease (CD) were reviewed. Most participants were adults. Some studies had a higher risk of having flaws, but most did not. A medicine called Certolizumab pegol (CZP) was found to work better than a sugar pill (placebo) in helping people with CD feel better. After 8 weeks, 26.9% of those taking CZP felt much better compared to 19.8% of those taking the placebo. Also, 40.2% of those taking CZP had their symptoms improve compared to 30.9% of those taking the placebo. However, more people taking CZP had serious side effects like getting sicker from CD, infections, or cancer. The chance of serious side effects was about 1.35 times higher for those taking CZP. We think CZP helps people with CD feel better, but we're not sure if it causes more serious side effects. More studies are needed to see how well CZP works long-term and if it's safe for everyone.

This review looked at different treatments to prevent something called post-operative recurrence in people who have Crohn's disease after surgery. The study found that:

- Probiotics, which are good bacteria, didn't seem to help.
- Nitroimidazole antibiotics, which are medicines that kill certain germs, seemed to help reduce the chance of both the disease coming back and needing a special test to look inside the body. But using these antibiotics might make it more likely to get serious side effects.
- Mesalamine, which is another medicine, seemed to help reduce the chance of the disease coming back and needing a special test. It also had fewer serious side effects.
- Azathioprine/6-MP, another type of medicine, also helped reduce the chance of the disease coming back and needing a special test. It had fewer serious side effects too.
- Infliximab, budesonide, tenovil, and interleukin-10 weren't studied enough to know if they work well.
- Nitroimidazole antibiotics, mesalamine, and azathioprine/6-MP all seemed to be better than probiotics for preventing the disease from coming back after surgery. But each has its own pros and cons, like how much it costs and how well it works with side effects. More research is needed to decide which one might be best.

output: This review looked at 10 studies with 484 patients to see if one treatment for removing small blood vessels (telangiectasias) worked better than others. The studies didn't show that any one treatment was clearly better than the others for treating these small blood vessels in the legs. However, the studies did find that getting treatment was better than not getting any treatment. Some treatments, like polidocanol (POL), caused more side effects when used at a higher strength, while others, like sodium tetradecyl sulfate (STS), were more painful. Polidocanol was also more painful than placebo. The studies didn't have enough information to compare how well different treatments work or how much patients liked them. The evidence isn't strong because the studies weren't very good. More research is needed to figure out which treatment works best and how to use it safely and effectively. Future studies should collect more information about who gets the treatment and how they feel about it.

output:
This review looked at 15 studies, mostly from China, that tested different medicines to help people who have trouble urinating. Many of these studies didn't follow good methods, so the results might not be very reliable. The studies mostly measured if the wet patches on pillows got smaller after taking the medicine. 

Some medicines like astemizole and diphenhydramine seemed to work better than a sugar pill, but the doses used can be dangerous. Propantheline also seemed to work, but the studies weren't consistent. Oryzanol, which comes from rice, and a Chinese medicine called suo quo wan also seemed to help more than another medicine called doxepin. 

However, there isn't enough strong evidence yet to know if these medicines really work better. The studies had many problems and it's hard to trust their results. But they still give us clues about what might work. To make sure, we need more carefully done studies. Right now, doctors shouldn't use these medicines unless they're part of a well-designed study.

output: The IQCODE test helps doctors spot older adults who might have dementia. In most studies, it correctly identified about 91 out of 100 people with dementia (high sensitivity) and correctly ruled out about 66 out of 100 people without dementia (high specificity). It's better at finding dementia in regular hospitals than in specialized memory clinics. The test works well whether it uses 16 or 26 questions. It doesn't matter much if the test is given in different languages. But the results might not apply to everyone because the studies had different numbers of people with dementia and some didn't report their methods clearly. So while the IQCODE can help find older adults who might have dementia, we need more studies to be sure it works the same way everywhere.

output: Three studies looked at different ways to treat people with a type of cancer called glioblastoma. These studies weren't done perfectly because they didn't hide which treatment the patients got, which means they might have had problems. But the studies themselves were done fairly well. One study found that giving radiation therapy (RT) along with a special medicine called PCV helped people live longer. This was discovered about 10 years after the study ended. The study also found that having certain changes in the DNA of the cancer cells (called codeletion of 1p and 19q or having mutations in IDH-1 or IDH-2 genes) can help doctors know which people might do better with this treatment. Giving PCV earlier, before or after radiation, seems to help people live longer. Using these DNA changes can help doctors find out who might benefit the most from this treatment. But PCV can cause serious side effects, so it's not clear if another medicine called temozolomide could replace it. More studies are needed to figure out the best way to use these DNA changes in treatment.

output: The review looked at 24 studies with 2126 participants to see if supportive therapy worked better than regular care for people with certain conditions. It found that supportive therapy didn't help prevent relapses or keep people out of the hospital. It also didn't seem to improve how people felt mentally or their satisfaction with the care they received. However, other types of therapy like cognitive behavioral therapy seemed to help reduce hospital stays and improve mental state. But the evidence for these differences is not very strong because it comes from just a few small studies. There's not enough information to say if supportive therapy works better than other types of therapy. Larger studies that focus on supportive therapy might give us clearer answers.

output: Three studies involving 123 people looked at whether having surgery to treat a condition was better than just using medicine. The studies didn't fully describe how they kept people from knowing who was getting which treatment, which makes it hard to know if the results are accurate. In two of the studies, it wasn't clear how they picked who got which treatment. None of the studies reported deaths, but six people died in total. The studies couldn't show if surgery was better or worse for survival. However, surgery seemed to help prevent some problems like pneumonia, chest deformities, and needing a tracheostomy. It also helped people get out of the hospital faster. But these benefits weren't always clear because the studies were small. More research is needed to see if these findings hold true and to find out if surgery affects survival.

output: Twenty studies looked at how well theophylline works for people with breathing problems. When compared to a sugar pill, theophylline helped people breathe better and their lungs worked harder. It also made it easier for people to take in oxygen and get rid of extra carbon dioxide. But it didn't help people walk farther or feel less breathless. Some people felt sick more often when taking theophylline, but others preferred it. Most people stayed in the studies, but the results might not apply to everyone because the people who stayed were probably already used to taking theophylline. Overall, theophylline seems to help a little bit with lung function and breathing, especially when used with other medicines. More studies are needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at six studies involving 355 infants to see if continuous distending pressure (CDP) helped them breathe better. Using CDP was linked to fewer babies needing to be put on machines to help them breathe (lower risk ratio (RR) 0.65, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.81) and lower overall death rates (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.87). It also seemed to lower death rates in babies born weighing more than 1500 grams (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.84). However, using CDP increased the chance of a baby getting a pneumothorax, which is a lung problem (RR 2.64, 95% CI 1.39 to 5.04). There was no clear difference in another condition called bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) or in how the babies were doing at 9 to 14 years old. The studies were done a long time ago, so it's hard to know if the results apply to modern practices. More research is needed to figure out the best way to use CDP for preterm babies who have trouble breathing.

output:
This review looked at 29 studies that examined policies to limit the use of certain medicines, mostly for older adults or those with lower incomes who rely on public programs for their medicine. Different types of medicines had different effects:

- For medicines that help with stomach problems and pain, limiting their use led to less medicine being taken and saved money, without people needing more doctor visits.
- For medicines that treat mental health issues, limiting their use made it harder for people to keep taking them and sometimes led to more doctor visits, but didn't save much money overall.
- For medicines that help lower blood pressure and reduce cholesterol, relaxing rules about who can get them made sure people got the right medicine and saved money.

Two studies looked at how these changes affected health, but the results weren't clear. Overall, limiting medicines can save money without making people need more doctor visits. But relaxing rules can help people get the right medicine too.

However, it's important to carefully plan these policies based on what the medicines do and how they affect people's health. Also, it's important to make sure everyone has fair access to these medicines, especially older adults and those with lower incomes.

output: This review looked at 15 studies with 1833 patients to see if different medicines used during surgery help patients wake up faster. The studies weren't all done well. Two studies showed that patients woke up slower after using isoflurane compared to propofol, but the difference wasn't big. Sevoflurane didn't seem to make patients wake up any faster or slower than propofol. Propofol seemed to cause fewer problems like feeling sick or having changes in blood pressure, but it might cause more changes in brain activity. Both isoflurane and propofol helped patients wake up faster than another medicine called isoflurane. The results are based on a few studies, so we're not very sure about them. More studies with better methods are needed to confirm these findings.

output:
This review looked at 15 studies to see if certain types of advice helped people with whiplash pain. Only three studies were considered to have done a good job of avoiding bias. 

For advice that helps people move around more, like watching a video, one study showed it might help reduce pain after a few months, but another study didn't find this helpful. Another study found a simple pamphlet about moving more wasn't better than a regular pamphlet. Overall, there's not much strong evidence that advice to move more helps with whiplash pain.

For advice on dealing with pain and stress, and making changes at work to be safer, the studies weren't clear enough to show if these worked or not. Some exercises for neck pain were found to be helpful for a short time, but self-care strategies like taking care of yourself didn't seem to help much.

Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say these types of advice help with whiplash pain. More research is needed that uses good methods to teach people these skills.

output: This review looked at 12 trials with 767 people to see if antibiotics helped stop diarrhea after they took them. The trials didn't find that antibiotics worked better than no medicine or a placebo for stopping diarrhea within two to four days. They also didn't find that antibiotics helped prevent diarrhea within five to seven days. Antibiotics didn't seem to help with other symptoms like fever or make the illness last longer. Antibiotics did help keep the bad bacteria from coming back in the first week. But, people who took antibiotics were more likely to have the bacteria come back one month later. Also, more people who took antibiotics had side effects. Overall, there's not enough good evidence to show that antibiotics help stop diarrhea caused by certain types of bacteria in healthy people. The results aren't clear for very young, very old people, or those with more serious cases. It seems that antibiotics might cause more problems than they solve.

output: This review looked at two small studies that tested how well Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS) works in predicting if pancreatic cancer can be removed completely. In these studies, 34 people were involved. The studies weren't perfect, but they didn't seem to have major problems. When doctors use CT scans to look for cancer, about 6 out of 10 people actually have cancer that can't be removed. EUS helps predict if the cancer can be removed, but it's not always right. If EUS says the cancer can't be removed, it's usually correct (about 87 out of 100 times), but if it says the cancer can be removed, it's not always right (about 80 out of 100 times). This means that about 13 out of 100 people who get good news from EUS might actually have cancer that can't be removed, and about 20 out of 100 people who get bad news might actually have cancer that can be removed. Because these studies are small, we're not sure if EUS is helpful in people with pancreatic cancer found to have potentially removable cancer on CT scans. We don't know if it helps in people with another type of cancer called periampullary cancer. Right now, there's not enough evidence to say that EUS should be done routinely for these types of cancer.

output: This review looked at nine studies with a total of 622 people who took a supplement called CrP along with exercises like lifting weights. The studies lasted up to 24 weeks. Some studies compared CrP with a placebo (a fake treatment), and others compared CrP at different doses. After 12 to 16 weeks, CrP seemed to help people lose a little bit of weight compared to taking a placebo. However, the evidence isn't strong enough to say which dose of CrP might work best or if it has any serious side effects. There's not enough good-quality evidence to know if CrP helps people lose weight or improves their health in other ways. More research is needed to make sure CrP is safe and effective for people trying to lose weight.

output: This review looked at one small study and three other studies that are still happening. The evidence from these studies is not very strong because it's hard to trust the results. The study compared two ways of giving blood to people with a type of blood problem called MDS. It didn't find clear differences in how well people did when given blood less often (restrictive policy) or more often (liberal policy). There wasn't enough information to know if one way was better than the other for things like how long people stay in the hospital or if they have more infections. The study also didn't look at serious problems like bleeding or infection. Because the study was small and not all the information was collected, we don't have enough good evidence to decide whether one way of giving blood is better for people with MDS. We need more studies with bigger groups of people to help us figure out the best way to give blood to these patients.

output: The review looked at eight studies with a total of 182 infants to see if a special formula with more medium-chain triglycerides (MCT) helped babies grow better than a regular formula. The studies didn't find any clear difference in how much the babies grew in terms of weight, length, head size, or fat under their skin. Some studies said the babies tolerated the MCT formula well, while others said it wasn't better. There was also no clear difference in how often babies got a condition called necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). The studies were too small to show if the MCT formula helps babies grow better in the long run or affects their brain development. More research is needed to know if the MCT formula is better for babies' growth or if it causes fewer problems. This includes looking at whether babies can tolerate the MCT formula better and if it affects how babies grow and develop over time.

output: This review looked at three studies with 451 participants to see if dexamethasone helped reduce nausea. Two studies compared dexamethasone to a sugar pill, and one compared different medicines. The studies lasted from 7 to 14 days. At 8 days, people who took dexamethasone had slightly less nausea than those who took a sugar pill, but this wasn't a big enough difference to be sure it wasn't just chance. The studies didn't have the same way to measure nausea, so it's hard to know if the results would apply to everyone. Some people had side effects, but not more than usual. Because the studies were small and didn't follow the same rules, the results aren't very strong. There isn't much research on using steroids to treat nausea in cancer patients besides chemotherapy and radiation. The evidence suggests that dexamethasone might help, but we need more studies to be sure.

output: This review looked at seven studies with 960 participants to see if putting a drain after surgery for breast cancer helps prevent a buildup of fluid called a seroma. The studies had some problems, so we can't be completely sure about the results. However, the studies suggested that drains might help reduce the number of times doctors need to remove fluid from the area. Drains also seemed to slightly lower the chance of another problem called a seroma forming. But using drains made people stay in the hospital longer. So while drains might help with some issues, they might also cause other problems. More high-quality studies are needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at two small studies of women who had an episiotomy wound that opened up and became infected after childbirth. The studies were not very good because they didn't use proper methods to make sure the results were reliable. One study found that women who had their wounds sutured again (re-sutures) might heal better at first, but this wasn't proven. Another study found that women who had re-sutures might start having sex sooner, but by six months, it didn't matter which group they were in. The studies didn't look at other important things like pain, how the wound looked, or how the mother felt about her recovery. Because the studies weren't strong, we don't know if re-sutures help or hurt. We need better studies to find out.

More research is needed to see if staying at home helps or hurts during PPROM. This is important because it could affect how healthcare is paid for in different places.

output: This review looked at nine studies involving 3144 people to see if linezolid worked better than vancomycin for treating skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs). Linezolid seemed to work better, especially for infections caused by a type of bacteria called MRSA. It helped clear up the infection faster and caused fewer side effects like itchy skin and rashes. People also spent less time in the hospital when taking linezolid. However, linezolid might cause more blood platelets to drop, which can be dangerous. The studies were funded by the company that makes linezolid, so they might have been biased. More studies are needed to confirm these findings.

This review looked at five small studies that tested different treatments for a condition called adhesive capsulitis, which causes shoulder pain and stiffness. The studies were not all the same and some did not report all the important details. Only one study was considered to have good quality. 

One study found that taking oral steroids (a type of medicine) helped reduce pain and improve shoulder movement in the short term, but these benefits did not last for six weeks. Another study didn't find a difference between taking steroids and taking a placebo pill. A third study found that taking steroids worked better to relieve pain right away, but the difference disappeared by five months.

Overall, the evidence suggests that taking oral steroids might help with shoulder pain and movement in the first few weeks, but it's not clear if it helps in the long run. There were few side effects reported. This means the evidence is not strong enough to recommend using steroids for adhesive capsulitis, but it might be helpful for a short time. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at 14 studies with 753 participants. It suggests that hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) might help wounds heal better in some cases of radiation-related problems like osteoradionecrosis (ORN) and radiation proctitis. HBOT seems to improve wound healing after operations for ORN and after surgeries like flaps and hemimandibulectomies. It also helps heal tooth sockets after radiation. However, it doesn't seem to help with problems in the brain or nerves. The studies were not perfect, so we're not sure if HBOT really works or if it has any bad side effects. More research is needed to see if HBOT is helpful and how best to use it.

output: This review looked at four studies involving a total of 1419 patients with a type of brain tumor called glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). The studies compared two treatments: giving a medicine called temozolomide along with radiation therapy versus just radiation therapy. Temozolomide seemed to help people live longer and helped their tumors grow more slowly. It also caused more side effects like feeling tired and getting sick. When temozolomide was given along with radiation in both the beginning and later stages, it worked better than just radiation. But when it was used after the first treatment didn't work, it didn't seem to help people live longer. For older patients, taking temozolomide alone didn't seem to help them live longer than just having radiation. The medicine also caused more side effects in older patients. Overall, temozolomide seems to be helpful in treating GBM, especially when given with radiation in both the start and later stages, but it causes more side effects.

output: This review looked at eight studies involving 996 people to see if certain medicines called corticosteroids helped prevent heart problems. The studies were done many years ago, from 1950 to 2001. They compared corticosteroids like prednisone and intravenous immunoglobulin with aspirin or no treatment. After one year, there wasn't much difference in the risk of heart disease between those taking corticosteroids and those taking aspirin. Some studies didn't tell us about any bad side effects, but others said there were serious ones. The studies were old and had some problems that made it hard to trust the results. There's not enough good evidence to say that corticosteroids help prevent heart problems in people with rheumatic fever. New studies are needed to look at these medicines and newer ways to treat heart problems in people with rheumatic fever. Better tools to check the health of the heart are also needed.

output: This review looked at 12 trials with 703 participants to see if treatments could help reduce fatigue after a stroke. Six of these trials had enough information to be combined and analyzed. They found that the treatments worked better than usual care in reducing fatigue, but the results varied between the studies. The treatments included medicines like fluoxetine and (-)-OSU6162, and non-medicine methods like learning about fatigue and doing stress reduction exercises. However, the benefits were not seen in trials that did a good job hiding which treatment was given or keeping the people measuring the results from knowing who got which treatment. No trials specifically looked at preventing fatigue. Some other trials that didn't focus on reducing fatigue did not show any benefit. Overall, there isn't strong evidence to support any specific treatment for reducing fatigue after a stroke. The trials were small and different, so more research with better designs and bigger groups is needed to find out what works best.

output: Two studies looked at whether low-level laser treatment helps improve numbness in the lips and chin after dental work. They found that some people felt their numbness improved after the laser treatment compared to when they got a fake treatment. However, the results weren't very clear because the studies were small and didn't follow all the patients. The studies also didn't look at other important things like pain or how well people could eat or speak. The evidence isn't very strong because the studies had some problems. We need more studies to see if laser treatment works better than other treatments for this numbness after dental work. These new studies should measure how much numbness improves, how much pain goes away, and ask people about their overall health and comfort.

output: This review looked at 20 studies with 2125 participants using different treatments for melasma. The studies couldn't be easily combined because the treatments were too different. Some treatments that worked better than others include a special cream with three ingredients (hydroquinone, tretinoin, and fluocinolone acetonide), azelaic acid, and a product called Thiospot. The triple-combination cream was much better at lightening melasma than just using hydroquinone alone. Azelaic acid was also better than 2% hydroquinone, but not as good as 4% hydroquinone. Tretinoin helped improve melasma in some cases, but not always. Thiospot was more effective than a placebo. Common side effects were mild and went away quickly. More high-quality studies are needed to know if these treatments work well and for how long.

output: This review looked at 43 studies involving 3497 people with dry eyes. The studies were different in how they were done, so it was hard to combine their results. Some artificial tears helped dry eye symptoms better than others, but the differences weren't always clear. One type called 0.2% polyacrylic acid worked better than another type called 1.4% polyvinyl alcohol in two studies. But other types didn't show clear differences. Most artificial tears seemed safe, but some caused side effects like feeling sick or dizzy. The studies had some problems, like not always telling us if something went wrong. There might be more studies out there, but we don't know the results. So, while some artificial tears might help dry eyes, we need more research to know which ones work best and if they're really safe.

output: This review looked at 22 studies that tested different hormonal methods to prevent pregnancy, using them in the vagina. These studies involved about 12,400 women in Europe, Asia, and the Americas. The studies tested levonorgestrel (LNG) in different doses and other hormonal drugs. The main findings were that using LNG in the vagina was effective and safe, with a low rate of getting pregnant. The most common side effect was changes in the period, but these didn't seem to happen more often if you took the pills more or less frequently. Most women liked using the vaginal method, even though their periods sometimes changed. While the studies were helpful, they had some problems. More recent research is needed to confirm if this method works well and is safe for women who don't have sex very often. If it proves to be good, doctors might change how they talk about birth control options.

output: This review looked at six trials from the 1970s that compared two medicines, chlorpromazine and piperacetazine, for treating schizophrenia. The trials were not very well done, and only short-term results were available. When doctors rated how much the patients improved, there was no clear difference between the two medicines. The medicines seemed to cause similar side effects, though about half of the people taking each medicine had some problems. No clear difference was seen in how many people left the study early. The results are based on very few people and are of very low quality. We don't have enough good information to know which medicine might work better. Clinicians and people with schizophrenia should talk to their doctor about the medicines, since there isn't strong evidence to choose one over the other. More high-quality research is needed to find out which medicine might be better.

output: Four studies looked at different ways to help people with HIV take their medicine better. One study found that a program where nurses visited people at home helped them remember to take their medicine more often. This made it easier for them to refill their prescriptions. But another study using diary cards didn't show a clear difference in how often people forgot to take their medicine. Another study with teen groups didn't find that the groups helped teens take their medicine better, but it did help more teens keep their virus under control. A third study found that kids taking a special medicine called LPV/r had better control of their virus than those taking a different kind of medicine. More research is needed to see which methods work best for helping kids take their medicine regularly and stay healthy.

output: This review looked at 34 studies with 2169 people who had blepharitis, a condition that causes itchy, red eyes. Some studies used different treatments like antibiotics and lid hygiene, which helps clean the eyelids. Antibiotics helped ease symptoms and get rid of bacteria for people with front blepharitis. Lid hygiene also helped people with both front and back blepharitis. But other treatments like topical steroids and oral antibiotics weren't proven to work better. Overall, there's not enough strong proof to say which treatments are best for chronic blepharitis. Many products sold for blepharitis aren't backed by good science. output: This review looked at different types of metal devices used to fix broken hips in older people. The Gamma nail and intramedullary hip screw (IMHS) were compared in 22 trials with 3749 participants. The Gamma nail was linked to more broken bones and needing more surgeries. Wound infections, death, and other health problems didn't differ much between the two types of screws. For IMHS and SHS, there weren't big differences in problems like wound infections or death. Some studies showed IMHS might cause more problems fixing the bone. Other studies comparing different types of nails didn't find clear differences. Two studies suggested IMHS might cause fewer problems with broken bones and faster recovery. Two other studies found IMHS might heal broken bones better than metal plates. The sliding hip screw (SHS) seems to work well for fixing broken hips, but more studies are needed to confirm this. Intramedullary nails might be better for some broken bones, but more research is needed to know for sure.

output: Three small studies looked at different types of physical therapy after a treatment called BoNT for people who have had a stroke and still have problems moving their arms. The studies were not very good because they had some flaws. The studies found that a special kind of therapy called modified constraint-induced movement therapy (mCIMT) helped people move their arms better and less stiff for up to six months. Also, using a special splint for the elbow and doing regular therapy helped keep the elbow joints from getting too tight. But another type of therapy called task practice therapy with a special electric stimulation didn't help more than just doing the usual therapy. None of the studies looked at children or people with leg problems. Overall, the evidence is not strong enough to say which types of therapy work best for helping arm movement after a stroke. We need more research to figure out the best kinds of therapy and how much is needed to help people move their arms better and feel better.

output: Six studies with 142 children with hemophilia showed that getting medicine regularly (prophylaxis) helps prevent bleeding episodes better than only using it when bleeding starts (on-demand treatment). Specifically, prophylaxis reduced bleeding into joints by about half compared to not using it at all. However, the studies couldn't agree on whether taking the medicine every day or waiting a week between doses works better. Studies in children with hemophilia A found that regular use of the medicine led to fewer joint bleeds. But studies comparing different dosing schedules didn't find one worked better than another. For hemophilia B, weekly injections were linked to fewer joint bleeds than bi-weekly ones. Using the medicine regularly also seemed to cause more problems like infections and blood clots. Strong evidence suggests that regular use helps keep joints healthy in children with hemophilia. But we need more studies to know if this is true for adults and if certain types of medicine work best.

output: This review looked at 13 studies with 975 people who had schizophrenia. The studies compared special programs to help people with schizophrenia improve their social skills with regular care. The programs seemed to work better. People who got the social skills programs had fewer times they had to go back to the hospital and felt better overall. Their lives were also better. But when the programs were compared to just talking groups, there wasn't much difference. The evidence isn't very strong because the studies weren't perfect. It's not clear if these programs would work the same way in other places. More research is needed to see if these programs help people with schizophrenia in different situations.

output: Seven studies looked at using sterile water instead of other liquids during labor to help with back pain. Most of these studies had good quality, but some had small groups of people, missing some data, or problems with how the study was done. The studies found that people who got sterile water had less back pain compared to those who got other liquids. However, it's hard to compare the results because the way pain was measured was different in each study. None of the studies looked at whether this helped with other important things like having a baby by cesarean section or needing extra medicine. Some women said they liked the pain relief better, but others didn't. There were no serious side effects. Because the studies weren't big enough or done well enough, we can't say for sure if sterile water helps with labor pain. More studies are needed to know if it works and if it has any other benefits or risks.

output: This review looked at seven studies comparing high and low levels of a breathing machine setting called PEEP in patients who have trouble breathing. In five studies, the researchers used the same amount of air each time a patient breathed in, but in two studies, the amount of air was different. Some of the studies had problems doing things fairly, but most were done well. When looking at studies where the same amount of air was used, there wasn't enough evidence to show that using higher levels of PEEP before a patient leaves the hospital helps or hurts their chances of survival. Higher levels of PEEP didn't seem to cause more breathing problems. It helped patients breathe better for the first few days, but didn't affect how long they stayed in the hospital. The studies also showed that patients with a condition called ARDS might do better if they use higher levels of PEEP, but this needs more research. Overall, the studies had some differences that make it hard to draw clear conclusions.

output: The review looked at eight studies that checked for broken bones in different types of healthcare settings. Most of these studies had some problems in how they were done. The studies found that about 6.5% to 11% of people who came to the emergency room and 0.7% to 4.5% of people who visited their doctor had broken bones. Some signs that might mean someone has a broken bone were checked in the studies, but not all of them worked well. The researchers found that three signs in doctors' offices were helpful, but the results weren't always clear. One sign in bigger hospitals was also helpful. Using more than one sign together was better at finding broken bones than using just one sign. The studies didn't find strong proof that checking for broken bones helps. But it seems that using a few signs together might help find broken bones. The signs aren't perfect though; they often show that someone has a broken bone when they don't. This means that if doctors use these signs, they might end up doing extra tests or treatments that don't really help. More research is needed to figure out the best signs to use and to make sure everyone knows how to use them correctly.

output: Two studies and one ongoing study looked at special programs to help Native American youth stop smoking or using smokeless tobacco. These programs included activities that fit with their culture. After 42 months, there wasn't much difference in how often the youth smoked or used smokeless tobacco compared to those who didn't get the special programs. Some youth did show less smoking or smokeless tobacco use after the programs, but it didn't last. The studies had some flaws, so we can't be sure if the programs work well. We don't have enough information to say if these programs help prevent smoking in young Native Americans. But we know that Native American youth start smoking earlier and smoke more than others, which means they face bigger health problems. More studies are needed to find out what works best to help young Native Americans avoid smoking.

output: This review looked at 32 studies comparing different types of culture media used during in vitro fertilization (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) to help embryos grow. Only a few studies provided enough information to combine their results. Of those, four found no difference between the types of media used for transferring embryos on day three or day five. One study suggested that a media called Quinn's Advantage might help more embryos survive if transferred on day three, but this study wasn't fully detailed. Other studies didn't find any differences in things like getting pregnant or having miscarriages. Most studies didn't tell us where they got their money or how they did their work. Because the studies weren't done well, we can't be sure which type of media works best. We need better studies to figure this out.

output: This review looked at ten studies where probiotics were used along with other medicines to treat fungal infections. The studies found that probiotics helped people get better faster and had fewer fungal infections during the first month. However, this didn't mean they stayed better longer. Probiotics did not help people stay better for longer periods of time. Using probiotics did not make it more likely that people would need extra medicine later or have serious side effects. While the studies suggest probiotics might help, the evidence isn't strong enough to be sure. More research is needed with bigger groups of people to know if probiotics really work better.

output: The review looked at 14 studies, but only 7 were strong enough to include. Four studies compared when implants were put in: right away or later. Two studies with 126 patients found no big difference between putting in the implants right away or waiting. One study with 46 patients found that people who got their implants right away thought it took less time to use them and were happier. But after 5 years, the people who got their implants right away had more problems. Another study with 16 patients found no difference between right away and waiting. Three studies looked at different ways to make space for implants in empty tooth sockets. One study with 26 patients found no difference if you use your own bone or special bone. Two studies with 56 patients found no difference in which way to fill the space. Overall, there isn't enough good evidence to say if putting in implants right away or waiting is better. Some studies suggest that right away implants might have more problems, but they look nicer right away. We don't know if we need to do extra work to prepare the space for implants or if one way is better than another. More studies are needed to find out.

output: This review looked at one small study that found that meditation might help improve the quality of life for patients who recently got sick with a blood disease that affects the blood cells. The study had some problems, like not knowing how many people were in it or their ages and genders. Because of these issues, we don't know if meditation really helps or not. The study showed that people who meditated felt less depressed compared to those who didn't meditate. But we don't have enough information to say if meditation changes how long someone lives, makes them feel less tired, or helps them sleep better. We need more studies to find out if meditation is helpful for people with blood diseases. Right now, we don't have enough good information to say if meditation works or not.
