output: This review looked at 37 studies with 3110 people who had a brain injury. Some new studies were added since the last time this was checked in 2009. The studies mostly gave people medicine to lower their body temperature right away after they got hurt. They kept giving the medicine for at least 24 hours. The studies looked at whether the medicine helped people live longer, if they had bad health problems later, or if they got pneumonia. But the results weren't always the same from one study to another. The studies didn't tell us enough about how well they were done, so we couldn't be sure if they were fair. The studies also had different ways of doing things, which made it hard to combine the results. We don't have strong proof that lowering body temperature helps people with brain injuries. We need more studies that are done better to find out if this treatment works.

output: This review looked at 11 studies that tested different ways to give chemotherapy drugs called anthracyclines. Seven studies looked at how long the medicine stayed in the body, and four studied how much medicine was given at once. Most of the studies involved adults with different types of cancer. The studies found that giving the medicine for at least six hours at a time seemed to help prevent heart problems caused by the medicine. This is good news because it means the medicine might be safer when given this way. However, the studies didn't find a clear difference in heart problems when the amount of medicine given at once was changed. More research is needed, especially in children, to see if giving the medicine for longer or in smaller amounts affects the heart.

output: The review looked at three studies in adults that lasted up to a week. These studies had 122 participants who were randomly assigned to get paracetamol along with strong opioid painkillers, but only 95 finished the treatment. The studies were small and had other problems that made it hard to trust their results. The studies didn't find any clear benefits of adding paracetamol to the usual pain medicines for reducing pain or improving quality of life. Paracetamol didn't seem to help more than a sugar pill. The studies also didn't show any clear side effects of using paracetamol. Because the studies had these issues, we don't have good enough evidence to say if paracetamol helps or hurts when used with other pain medicines for people with cancer. More studies with better methods are needed to learn if paracetamol might help more with pain.

output: This review looked at eleven different campaigns aimed at reducing smoking. Some of these campaigns worked better than others. In two places, California and Massachusetts, where big campaigns were done, fewer people started smoking compared to other parts of the country. In three of the seven campaigns that looked at how much people smoked, there were fewer cigarettes being smoked. Four out of eight campaigns that looked at whether people stopped smoking showed some success. But in one campaign, the success was because more people who had quit smoking and those who still smoked were counted together. Overall, it seems that big campaigns using TV, radio, and newspapers can help reduce smoking among adults. However, the results are mixed because the campaigns were different in how they were done and how long they lasted. Some campaigns worked well for a while, but others didn't have lasting effects. The campaigns seemed to work better in some places than others, but it's hard to know why.

output: This review looked at seven studies with a total of 422 people who took trifluoperazine instead of a less powerful antipsychotic drug. The studies were not always done in a way that makes the results very reliable. Trifluoperazine didn't seem to work better than the less powerful drugs for making people feel better. But it didn't make people feel worse either. It did cause more movement problems like stiffness and jerky movements. The studies were small and not very good, so we can't be sure if these movement problems are common or just happened by chance. We don't have enough information about other important things like whether it helps people live longer or feel better. More studies with better methods are needed to know if trifluoperazine works better or worse than the less powerful drugs.

output: This review looked at 11 studies where people with moderate to severe pain took different types of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for one week or longer. About 949 people took part, but many didn't finish the study or report their results. Most studies weren't done well enough to trust the results. The studies compared different NSAIDs, but not all NSAIDs against each other or against opioids. The results aren't very reliable because the studies had problems like not keeping participants blind to which treatment they got or not having enough people in the studies. The studies didn't show if NSAIDs helped people feel less pain, especially if the pain was very bad. Some people had side effects like feeling thirsty, losing their appetite, feeling sleepy, or having stomach problems. Many people stopped taking the medicine because it wasn't working or because of side effects. Overall, there isn't strong proof that NSAIDs help people with cancer pain get better. But some people might find some relief quickly, though we can't be sure how much or if it lasts.

output: This review looked at two studies involving a total of 281 pregnancies and 282 fetuses. The studies had different methods and some didn't follow the same rules, so it wasn't possible to combine their results. One study found that taking a combination of hormones called oestrogen and progestogen did not help prevent miscarriages, perinatal deaths, or preterm births compared to taking a placebo. Another study, which looked at IVF pregnancies, also found no difference in miscarriage rates between those taking the hormone combination and those not taking it. Both studies found that the hormone combination might slightly increase the risk of cancer in the mother's reproductive system. However, there was no difference in other health outcomes like low birth weight or cancer in the baby. Because the studies had limitations, we don't have enough strong evidence to say whether taking these hormones helps prevent miscarriages. More research is needed to find out.

output: This review looked at 10 studies with a total of 1049 people. Most studies compared different treatments for a condition called Bullous Pemphigoid (BP). Some studies found that getting more steroid treatment through a process called plasma exchange might help control BP better than just taking steroids. Other studies didn't find a difference in how well different types of steroids worked. Some studies found that using a stronger steroid cream was better than taking a lot of oral steroids, but it might cause more side effects. Using a weaker steroid cream was found to be safe and effective. Studies also found that starting with a higher dose of oral steroids didn't help more and lower doses might work just as well. Adding other medicines like azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil to steroids didn't seem to help much. More research is needed to see if these added medicines work.

output: Two trials involving 269 participants looked at using CPAP or bilevel NPPV instead of oxygen therapy for adults with acute respiratory failure after upper abdominal surgery. The trials were done in China and Italy, and mostly involved men aged 65 years old. Both trials had some problems in how they were done, so we're not sure how reliable their results are. The trials found that CPAP or bilevel NPPV might help reduce the need for a breathing tube (tracheal intubation) by about half (RR 0.25), which means fewer people would need it. It also might help people stay in the ICU for a shorter time (MD -1.84 days). But the trials didn't show if this helped people live longer or if it made their hospital stay shorter. The trials didn't find clear evidence that it helped prevent leaks in the stomach area, lung problems, or infections. One trial found that bilevel NPPV might make blood tests show better breathing (PaO2 and pH levels) one hour after the treatment. More well-designed studies are needed to confirm these findings. Using CPAP or bilevel NPPV seems to be helpful and safe for treating this condition, but we need more research to be very confident about its benefits.

output: This review looked at different treatments for a condition called Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS), but it had some problems. It didn't have clear ways to diagnose TOS, so the researchers used how they diagnosed it in their studies. The review found one study comparing TOS getting better on its own with a treatment. It also found three studies that compared different treatments, but only two lasted long enough to be included. One study compared a surgery called transaxillary first rib resection (TFRR) with another called supraclavicular neuroplasty of the brachial plexus (SNBP). This study had some issues, but TFRR seemed to help reduce pain more than SNBP. There were no bad side effects in either group. Another study compared a treatment using a special medicine called botulinum toxin (BTX) to a placebo. The BTX treatment helped with tingling feelings after six months, but didn't make pain or disability better. There were no bad side effects from the BTX treatment. Because of the lack of clear ways to diagnose TOS, the review couldn't say for sure if TFRR or BTX is better than no treatment. There's not much evidence about other treatments either. The review suggests that doctors need to agree on how to diagnose TOS and use the same way to measure how well treatments work. They also need to do better studies to compare treatments with no treatment and with each other.

output: This review looked at four studies that compared professional oral care with regular oral care in nursing homes. The studies had some flaws, so we can't be very sure about their results. None of the studies found that professional oral care reduced the number of times people got pneumonia. However, one study suggested that it might help prevent pneumonia-related deaths. It's not clear if professional oral care reduces all deaths in nursing homes. The studies didn't find many side effects from professional oral care. While professional oral care might help prevent pneumonia, we don't know if it works better than regular care. We also don't have good evidence on which specific oral care methods work best. More studies are needed to learn more about this.

output: This review looked at five studies with 1330 participants. None of the studies looked at shorter treatment periods. One study added levofloxacin to a standard treatment for 174 people, but it didn't report on whether the treatment worked better or worse. Another three studies replaced different medicines in the standard treatment with fluoroquinolones for 723 people. They didn't find clear evidence that adding fluoroquinolones helped or hurt in terms of death, getting better, or side effects. One study replaced isoniazid with moxifloxacin for 433 people, but it didn't report on relapse or serious side effects. Studies testing shorter treatment periods with fluoroquinolones are still ongoing. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say if adding or replacing fluoroquinolones in the standard treatment helps or hurts in treating tuberculosis. More research is needed to get clearer answers.

output: This review looked at ten trials with 1658 participants to see if a special breathing technique called "open lung ventilation" helped people with a condition called Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS). Five out of the ten trials were considered to have done a good job to avoid bias. The trials found that this technique might help reduce deaths in the ICU, but it didn't seem to affect deaths within 28 days or during hospital stays. It also didn't cause more lung injuries. However, because the trials varied in how they did the breathing technique, it's hard to know if the results apply to everyone. The evidence is of low quality because the trials often used other treatments along with the breathing technique, which could have affected the results. So, while this technique might help in some cases, we need more research to be sure.

output: This review looked at five studies with a total of 207 people who had different treatments for a blocked colon. The studies compared a procedure called colorectal stenting with emergency surgery. The surgery seemed to work better because it helped people feel better faster. On average, people who had surgery felt better after 3.55 days, while those who got the stent took about 1 day. About 86 out of 100 stents went in successfully. Both treatments had similar chances of dying within 30 days, around 2 out of 100. About 6 out of 100 stents broke or moved. The surgery took longer, but people stayed in the hospital for fewer days. The stent group lost less blood during the procedure. While the surgery was better at making people feel better quickly, the stent didn't seem to cause more problems. It might be safer and easier to do than surgery. But more studies are needed to be sure.

output: This review looked at 15 studies with a total of 1048 people who had mild to moderate asthma. Most studies were done in India and Europe. The studies mostly involved adults with asthma for 6 months to over 23 years. Some of the studies used yoga breathing alone, while others included yoga practices like posture and meditation. The studies lasted from 2 weeks to 54 months, with most lasting less than 6 months. Some of the studies had a higher risk of having biases. The studies showed that yoga might help improve quality of life, symptoms, and reduce the amount of medicine people take for their asthma. The improvements in quality of life were noticeable, but it's not clear if the changes in symptoms were big enough to matter. Yoga didn't seem to affect how well people could breathe out quickly. There were no serious side effects reported, but the information on this wasn't very complete. Overall, the evidence suggests that yoga might help asthma, but we're not sure how much. More studies with lots of people and better ways of doing the studies are needed to be really confident.

output: This review looked at five studies comparing different methods to place a tube into an artery in children. Ultrasound guidance, where a machine helps doctors see inside the body, was better at putting the tube in the first time compared to using touch alone (palpation) or listening with a special tool (Doppler auditory assistance). Ultrasound guidance also led to fewer problems like bleeding around the area. However, the studies weren't perfect because some didn't hide who got which method well enough. The evidence is considered moderate, meaning it's not very precise but still suggests ultrasound helps. It seems ultrasound works best for younger children and those who have trouble getting the tube in the first time. More studies are needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at 12 studies involving 7,119 participants. Most studies had a moderate risk of having flaws that might affect the results. Some studies compared putting an IUD right away versus putting it later. One study found that putting the Copper 7 IUD right away was linked with a higher chance of it coming out compared to putting it later. The chances of the IUD coming out or getting pregnant were higher if it was put right away instead of later in five studies. Another study suggested that a different type of IUD called Nova T might lead to more women getting pregnant. Overall, the studies show that putting an IUD right away after an abortion is safe and practical. But the IUD comes out more often if it's put right away after an abortion compared to putting it later. At six months after an abortion, more women use the IUD if it was put right away.

output: Two small studies looked at how well exercise helped people with chronic venous insufficiency (CVI). Both studies measured how much better people felt and how their legs worked after exercising. One study found that people who exercised had less swelling and their hearts pumped blood better than those who didn't exercise. The other study didn't find a difference. Both studies had some problems being fair, so we shouldn't trust the results too much. Because there weren't many studies and not enough people were in them, we don't know if exercise really helps. More research is needed to see if exercise works for people with CVI, and it should look at different types of exercises and how often people do them.

output: This review looked at 11 studies involving 471 people with antisocial personality disorder (AsPD), but only 276 people had complete information. Different types of talking therapies were tested, but not all studies measured the same things. Some studies found that combining a type of therapy called cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) with regular care helped people with cocaine addiction. Other studies found that adding contingency management (which involves rewards for good behavior) to regular care might help people who have recently had violent incidents. But it didn't always work. A special program that combines motivational interviewing (a way to encourage people to change their behavior) with time in jail helped people who drive drunk. While some therapies seemed to help with substance use, none clearly reduced antisocial behaviors like aggression or reoffending. Few studies looked at whether these therapies worked for all aspects of antisocial personality disorder. Overall, there's not enough strong evidence to recommend any specific therapy for AsPD. More research is needed to find effective treatments.

output: This review looked at four studies that compared taking a hormone called glucocorticoid during a fertility treatment called IVF. Only two studies had enough information to be included in the analysis. The studies didn't find a clear difference in how often women got pregnant or had a baby after taking the hormone. The studies were small and had limited information, so it's hard to know if the hormone helps or not. If we assume that about 15 out of 100 women get pregnant without the hormone, adding the hormone might make it about 7 to 31 out of 100. Similarly, if we assume about 24 out of 100 women get pregnant without the hormone, adding the hormone might make it about 23 to 47 out of 100. The studies didn't find much difference in having twins or miscarriages. Also, the studies didn't report on side effects or a condition called OHSS, which can happen during IVF. Overall, we don't have enough good evidence to say if the hormone helps or hurts IVF success. More research is needed to better understand its effects.

output: This review looked at four trials with 15,936 people who had high blood pressure. The average age was 75 years. At the start, their blood pressure was about 171/86 mmHg. The trials didn't show that taking a medicine called hawthorn helped prevent memory problems (dementia) or made people's thinking better. However, the medicine did lower both the top and bottom numbers of people's blood pressure. Some people had to stop taking the medicine because of side effects, but it didn't happen more often than with a sugar pill. The trials had some problems, like not knowing if some people in the placebo group were getting the real medicine anyway. So, the evidence isn't strong enough to say that lowering blood pressure helps prevent memory problems in older adults with high blood pressure. More studies might give clearer answers.

This review looked at two small studies that compared a hormone treatment called LHRH agonist (either leuprorelin or decapeptyl) with another treatment (treosulfan or placebo) for women with a type of cancer called ovarian cancer that has come back after treatment with chemotherapy. The studies did not have enough information to combine their results into one big picture. 

For how long the cancer stays away (progression-free survival) and how long a person lives (overall survival), the studies didn't show much difference between the two treatments. Some side effects like hair loss and feeling tired might happen more often with one treatment than the other, but it's hard to know for sure because the studies weren't designed to look at these things. 

The studies also didn't report on how well people felt (quality of life) or if the treatments caused serious problems. Because the studies were small and the information wasn't clear, we don't have enough good evidence to say whether LHRH agonists are helpful or harmful for this type of ovarian cancer. The information we do have is very uncertain, so we can't make strong statements about the safety or effectiveness of these treatments. More research is needed to better understand how well these treatments work.

output: In this review, 55 studies with 16,154 people who have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) were looked at. Most studies found that using inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) for more than six months didn't help keep their lung function from getting worse. However, one big study showed it might help a little bit. Using ICS didn't seem to affect how long people lived. Studies that could pool their results showed that people using ICS had fewer flare-ups of COPD. ICS also seemed to improve how well people felt overall. But, ICS didn't work better for everyone. It didn't depend on whether people got better with oral steroids, if their lungs opened up easily with a puff of air, or if their airways were extra sensitive. Using ICS did make some people more likely to get a fungal infection in their mouth and hoarse voices. Also, people taking ICS had a higher chance of getting pneumonia. Overall, the studies didn't show a clear benefit for bones. The review suggests that people with COPD should talk to their doctors about whether using ICS might help them feel better and have fewer flare-ups, even though there might be some risks involved.

output: This review looked at 11 studies about using antibiotics for colds and stuffy noses. Six studies looked at colds, and five studied stuffy noses. Some studies didn't tell us everything they did, so we're not sure if they were done fairly. Antibiotics didn't seem to help people get over colds faster or keep their colds from coming back. In fact, some people might feel worse after taking them. For stuffy noses, antibiotics might make it a little less stuffy, but not much. There's a chance that antibiotics might cause more problems than they solve. So, doctors don't usually give antibiotics for colds or stuffy noses unless there's a clear reason to do so.

This review looked at three small studies that tried different ways to treat high potassium levels in premature babies. Only one study could tell us if the treatment worked better than a placebo. The studies had some problems, like not hiding which treatment the babies got or not making sure the doctors knew which baby was getting which treatment. 

One study found that giving babies insulin and sugar might help lower their potassium levels and reduce the chance of a serious brain injury. Another study found that breathing in albuterol might also help lower potassium levels. Neither of these studies showed that using a special medicine called cation-exchange resin helped. 

There were no serious side effects from any of the treatments. The studies were too small and not very well done to give clear advice about which treatment works best. Based on these studies, it seems that giving insulin and sugar might be better than using the special medicine for treating high potassium levels in premature babies. More studies are needed to see if breathing in albuterol helps and if it's as good as or better than insulin and sugar. Other treatments that might work are not yet studied.

Another study, which wasn't as detailed, showed similar results for another medicine called dalteparin. Both studies had some problems, so we don't have strong proof yet that these medicines work better than a sugar pill. More studies are needed to know if these medicines help with pain in people with sickle cell disease.

output: This review looked at eight studies with 21,379 people who have diabetes. Some studies compared ticlopidine to aspirin or nothing, and others compared clopidogrel to aspirin or another medicine. Most studies looked at people who already had heart problems. The studies were fairly good at following their participants. The studies lasted from about 3 years to almost 9 years. Only one study looked at whether these medicines helped prevent death from any cause, heart problems, or heart attacks. This study didn't find any clear difference. Another study looked at strokes and found no clear difference either. There wasn't enough information to look at other things like heart attacks, leg pain, or how well people felt. Also, the studies didn't always tell us if the people taking the medicines had diabetes. So, we don't have strong evidence to say these medicines work better than others for preventing heart problems in people with diabetes. We need more studies that focus just on people with diabetes to know more.

output: This review looked at one study involving 176 women. The study compared two ways of caring for new mothers and their babies: letting the baby stay close to the mom (rooming-in) and keeping the baby in a different room (separate care). The study found that babies in both groups were breastfed for about four months, but there wasn't much difference between the groups. Rooming-in didn't seem to make babies breastfeed longer. However, babies in the rooming-in group were breastfed more often on the first day after birth. When the babies left the hospital, more in the rooming-in group were still being fed only breast milk. But it's hard to know if this difference means anything because the babies in the separate care group were always given breast milk at the same time each day. Overall, the study doesn't strongly support or rule out the idea that letting babies stay with their moms more often helps with breastfeeding. More studies are needed to better understand this.

output: This review looked at 11 studies with a total of 821 people. Two studies were still being reviewed, and one study was ongoing. Some studies used green tea, and others used black tea. The ongoing study uses green tea in capsule form. No studies reported heart problems. Black tea was found to lower LDL cholesterol (a type of bad cholesterol) and blood pressure after six months. However, only a few studies showed these results, and it's hard to know if the findings are reliable because the studies might have had some flaws. Green tea also lowered LDL cholesterol and blood pressure, but again, only a few studies showed these results, and the findings weren't always consistent. When both green and black tea were studied together, they showed similar benefits. Side effects were rare and not clearly linked to the tea. While the evidence suggests that drinking tea might help prevent heart disease, there aren't many long-term studies. More high-quality research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at four studies involving 388 women who had forceps deliveries. The studies used different ways to measure pain relief and different medicines, so we couldn't combine the results. In one small study, women who got diazepam said their pain was better than those who got another medicine called vinydan-ether. Another small study didn't find a big difference between diazepam and another medicine called ketamine. In a third study, women who got a special kind of medicine put near their nerves felt better pain than those who got medicine put near their vagina. This study also found that women who got the special nerve medicine had less severe pain during the delivery. However, the studies didn't look at serious problems for mom or baby. Women who got diazepam were less likely to throw up compared to those who got vinydan-ether. But the studies didn't look at other important things like how well the babies did after birth. Overall, there isn't enough good evidence to say which medicine or way of giving medicine works best for pain during forceps deliveries. We also don't know much about how it affects babies.

output:
This review looked at three small studies that tested different combinations of vitamins for people with retinitis pigmentosa (RP), a condition that affects vision. The studies included people of different ages, from 4 to 55 years old, who all had RP because of their genes. 

None of the studies reported how well the vitamins helped improve vision over time. Also, none of the studies reported any bad side effects from taking the vitamins. 

The studies didn't show that taking vitamin A or DHA alone or together helped stop vision from getting worse. Some studies found that the vitamins might help a little bit in certain groups of people, but these findings weren't consistent across all the studies. 

So, based on these studies, there's no clear proof that taking vitamin A or DHA helps people with RP keep their vision better. Future studies should look at whether the vitamins work differently in people who have taken them before, and make sure they have enough people in the study to see if the vitamins really help.

output: This review looked at 26 trials comparing a medicine called salmeterol to a placebo (a dummy pill) and 8 trials comparing it to another asthma medicine called salbutamol. It involved 62,815 people with asthma, including 2,599 children. In some trials, they couldn't find information about serious side effects. Salmeterol didn't seem to cause more serious health problems overall, but it did seem to cause more serious side effects like hospitalizations. For every 188 people taking salmeterol, one extra person had a serious side effect over 28 weeks. The review couldn't tell if children had different risks than adults. When comparing salmeterol to salbutamol, there wasn't enough evidence to show it caused more serious side effects. The review found that people who took salmeterol without using inhaled corticosteroids (a common asthma treatment) had a higher chance of dying from their asthma. This was true even though the confidence intervals were wide, so we can't be sure that inhaled corticosteroids completely protect against this risk. The review also found that salmeterol might increase the risk of serious side effects. The study in children had too few participants to give clear answers.

This review looked at four studies involving 522 women. Most studies compared different doses of hCG (a hormone) given before in vitro fertilization (IVF). The studies had some problems in how they were done, making it hard to trust the results fully. 

When comparing 10,000 units of hCG to no hCG, there was no clear difference in how many women got pregnant or had miscarriages. Some studies found a slightly lower chance of getting pregnant, but the results weren't strong enough to be sure. Other studies didn't have enough information to make a judgment. 

There wasn't enough information to know if giving 20,000 units of hCG instead of 10,000 units made a difference. No studies reported on side effects or if the hormone caused any problems. 

Overall, the evidence suggests that hCG might slightly lower the chances of getting pregnant during IVF, but we don't know for sure. More studies are needed to better understand the effects of hCG and the best way to use it.

output: This review looked at 13 studies with 2341 participants to see if using ultrasound helps when putting a tube into a vein. Most of the studies weren't very good at showing they were fair. For the neck vein (subclavian vein), ultrasound helped reduce the chance of accidentally hitting an artery and forming a blood clot. It didn't seem to help much with other problems like bleeding or needing more tries. For the leg vein (femoral vein), ultrasound made it easier to put the tube in on the first try, but it wasn't clear if this made a big difference overall. The studies weren't sure about whether ultrasound helped with bigger problems like death or how well people felt. Overall, using ultrasound seems to make the process safer and better for putting in veins, especially for the neck vein. But we don't know if it works as well for everyone or for people who might have more trouble.

This review looked at four trials involving 494 participants. The trials found that using a 10-mg warfarin plan helped more people reach a good blood-thinning level (INR) within five days compared to a placebo. This was true for both people staying in the hospital and those going home. However, the benefit was less clear for people taking a 5-mg plan. 

Using either plan did not seem to make a big difference in how often people had dangerous blood clots or bleeding problems after 90 days. It also didn't affect how long people stayed in the hospital. 

There's some uncertainty about whether a 10-mg or 5-mg plan works better. Different studies had different numbers of people and followed them for different lengths of time, which made it hard to know for sure. More research is needed to find the best way to start warfarin for people with blood clots.

output: This review looked at 14 studies with 1,724 participants who had chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), which includes ear infections and other conditions. The studies used different ways to define and measure CSOM, and some didn't handle both ears equally. When comparing treatments, topical quinolone antibiotics cleared ear discharge faster than no treatment or antiseptics at one week. However, there wasn't a clear difference between quinolone and non-quinolone antibiotics at one or three weeks. At two weeks, quinolone antibiotics seemed to work better, but this might be because of just one study. Quinolone antibiotics were also better at curing CSOM than antiseptics at one week and two to four weeks. But the effects of non-quinolone antibiotics (without steroids) compared to antiseptics weren't always clear. The evidence about safety was weak. Overall, topical quinolone antibiotics seem to be better at clearing ear discharge than other treatments. However, the effects of non-quinolone antibiotics are less clear, and more studies are needed to see if they're as good or if they have fewer side effects.

output: This review looked at three small studies that compared different ways to help patients feel less pain after a type of surgery called robotic radical prostatectomy. The studies involved mostly men who were 50 to 75 years old. They found that using propofol, a medicine that helps you sleep, might help reduce pain after surgery, especially in the first few hours. Propofol might also help keep your tummy from getting too big during the surgery, which can sometimes happen. However, the studies were small and didn't look at everything, like if the medicines caused problems or if the patients got better faster. Because the studies weren't very big or detailed, we don't know if propofol is better than another medicine used during surgery for this type of surgery. More studies are needed to find out which medicine works best for everyone.

output: Six studies involving 394 children with enlarged adenoids showed that using corticosteroids in the nose helped reduce their stuffy noses and made their adenoids smaller. Different types of corticosteroids were tested, and some worked better than others. Beclomethasone, a type of corticosteroid, seemed to work well, reducing symptoms and making adenoids smaller more than a placebo. Mometasone and flunisolide also helped reduce adenoids and symptoms, but not as much as beclomethasone. Fluticasone was the best, helping 76 out of 100 children avoid adenoid surgery compared to only 20 out of 100 who used a salt water spray. However, one study didn't see these benefits with beclomethasone. While these results suggest corticosteroids can help, more research is needed to know if they work long-term.

output: This update includes four new studies, bringing the total to 12 studies with 461 participants. All studies had high or unclear risks of bias. The quality of the evidence was low to very low, partly because the studies were small and had other limitations. Two small studies comparing LASB (local anaesthetic sympathetic block) to placebo or sham treatment did not show that LASB helped reduce pain in the short term. One small study found that LASB might help reduce pain after one year, but not in the short term. Another study that added LASB to rehabilitation didn't show any extra benefit. Studies comparing LASB to other treatments didn't find a clear difference in pain relief. One study found no difference between guided and unguided LASB. Adverse events were mostly minor. The overall picture hasn't changed much from earlier reviews. There isn't enough good-quality evidence to say if LASB works or not for Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS). The limited information suggests that LASB doesn't seem to be effective for reducing pain in CRPS. More research is needed.

output: This review looked at 25 studies with 5218 women to see if being upright and moving around during labor helps. In most cases, women who stood up and moved around had their babies about an hour and a half faster than those who stayed in bed. These women were also less likely to need a cesarean section or an epidural. Their babies were less likely to need to go to the special baby room after birth. However, the studies weren't all done the same way, so we need more research to be sure. Overall, it seems that standing up and moving around during labor can help make the process easier for both mom and baby. But more high-quality studies are needed to be completely confident. So, doctors should tell moms about the benefits and help them move around as much as they want.

output: This review looked at 21 studies with 884 people to see if different treatments helped with wrist pain and problems. Hand braces helped reduce pain and make it easier to use the hand after four weeks. Ultrasound treatment didn't help much right away, but after seven weeks it did help. Taking medicines like steroids or diuretics for two weeks helped reduce pain. Vitamin B6 and yoga also helped reduce pain after eight weeks. Carpal bone mobilization, which is a special type of massage, helped reduce pain after three weeks. Steroid shots and insulin injections for people with diabetes helped reduce pain over eight weeks. Using special keyboards didn't seem to help much. Magnet therapy, laser acupuncture, and other types of physical therapy didn't show clear benefits. Right now, taking steroids, using a splint, ultrasound, yoga, and carpal bone mobilization seem to work well in the short term. But more studies are needed to know if these treatments last longer and if one is better than another.

output: This review looked at 24 studies, but only 16 with enough information to analyze. It found that neither estrogen replacement therapy (ERT) nor hormone replacement therapy (HRT) helped prevent memory problems in older women over the first few years of treatment. Some studies showed that ERT might make memory worse after just one year, and HRT might make it worse after three or four years. Most studies didn't find any clear benefits for different parts of memory. Overall, the evidence suggests that ERT and HRT don't help prevent memory problems in older women who take them for a short time or longer. We don't know if certain types of ERT or HRT work better for different groups of women. Larger studies are needed to figure out if any of these factors might make a difference. Until then, doctors shouldn't recommend ERT or HRT for the purpose of improving memory in older women who already have memory issues.

output: This review looked at seven trials with 1369 participants. Most of the trials had problems in how they were done, which means the results might not be completely reliable. The trials mostly studied people with a type of liver infection called hepatitis C. They found that continuing treatment for 72 weeks instead of 48 weeks helped more people have their infection go away completely. This happened whether the doctors used one way to tell if someone was a "slow responder" or another way. Longer treatment didn't help people stay on their medicine better. But it's important to note that the trials didn't look at how many people died or how well the treatment worked for other things. Also, the information about side effects wasn't always clear. So, while this suggests that longer treatment might work better for some people, we need more studies to know for sure.

output: This study looked at whether getting special pictures of the brain right after surgery helps people with a type of brain tumor called glioblastoma live longer. The study involved 125 people who had surgery for this type of tumor. The researchers found that getting these pictures soon after surgery didn't seem to make a big difference in how long people lived. The study wasn't perfect because it might have had some problems. There's not enough good information to know if getting these pictures sooner helps or hurts. The study also didn't look at costs or other ways the pictures might affect people. More research is needed to figure out the best time to get these pictures after surgery for people with glioblastoma. This could involve using computer models to better understand when to check the brain after surgery.

output: This review looked at 21 studies with 6253 participants, mostly from the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s. The Functional Rating Scale (FRS) helps doctors tell if someone has schizophrenia, but it's not perfect. It correctly identifies people with schizophrenia about 75% to 95% of the time. This means that sometimes it might say someone has schizophrenia when they don't, and sometimes it might miss someone who really does have it. When doctors use FRS to quickly decide who needs more help, they might wrongly think 5 to 19 out of every 100 people with FRS showing signs have schizophrenia. This could mean some people who need help might wait longer, and others who don't need it might leave too soon. Using FRS carefully, even with its limitations, can help avoid many of these mistakes. Newer tests might do better, but FRS is still a useful tool for spotting schizophrenia quickly.

This review looked at 13 studies involving 5686 patients to see if using a special machine called a PAC (which helps doctors monitor blood flow and pressure in patients) made a difference in how sick patients did in the hospital. Most of the studies had some problems keeping things fair, like not making sure everyone knew who was getting the PAC or who was getting the regular care. 

When looking at all the studies together, the PAC didn't seem to make a big difference in how long it took for patients to get better or how long they stayed in the hospital. It also didn't seem to save money overall. 

However, the studies weren't perfect, so we're not completely sure if the PAC really doesn't help. More studies are needed to figure out if there's a way to use the PAC that might help patients get better faster or spend less time in the hospital.

output: This review looked at six studies with a total of 788 women to see if natural cycle IVF was better than standard IVF. The studies didn't find a clear difference in how many babies were born alive (live birth rates) or how many got sick (OHSS) between the two types of IVF. The studies also didn't show much difference in the chances of having twins or triplets, or in the chances of getting pregnant again after the first time. Some studies found that fewer eggs were retrieved in the natural cycle group, but it's hard to know if this is important. The evidence isn't very strong because the studies had small numbers of women or weren't done very well. More research is needed to see if natural cycle IVF works better or worse than standard IVF. Future studies should look at more things like how many treatments are needed to get a baby, how much it costs, and any side effects.

output: Three trials involving 244 women looked at using prostaglandins to help remove the placenta after childbirth. The studies had some problems in how they were done, so we can't be very sure about their results. The prostaglandins did not seem to reduce the need for manual removal of the placenta, severe bleeding, or the need for blood transfusions. However, they did seem to cause more shivering in some women. The prostaglandins didn't affect the amount of blood lost or how quickly the placenta came out. The trials were not very good, so we're not confident in these results. We don't have enough strong evidence to know if prostaglandins are better than other methods. More well-designed studies are needed to find out if prostaglandins are helpful or harmful.

output: Two studies looked at how paying dentists differently might affect their work. One study found that dentists who were paid extra for each tooth they fixed were more likely to do more work. But this study only looked at the poorest areas and the results might not apply everywhere. The other study compared two ways of paying dentists: one where they got a set amount each year (capitation) and another where they got paid for each visit (fee-for-service). Dentists who got paid per visit saw fewer patients and did fewer fillings and teeth removals, but gave more advice to prevent problems. However, the studies didn't look at whether these changes helped patients more or less. The evidence isn't strong because there weren't many studies, and the quality of the evidence is low. More research is needed to see if changing how dentists are paid affects their work and if it helps patients.

output: This review looked at three studies that involved 285 premature babies. The studies found that giving arginine, a type of amino acid, might help prevent a condition called necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) in these babies. Babies who got arginine had a lower chance of developing NEC compared to those who didn't get it. The studies showed that arginine might reduce the risk of NEC stage 1 and stage 3, and it might also lower the risk of dying from NEC. However, the studies had some limitations, like having a small number of babies in each group. While arginine seems helpful, more research is needed to confirm these findings. At this time, there isn't enough evidence to make a strong recommendation about using arginine to prevent NEC in premature babies. More studies are needed to better understand the benefits and risks.

output: This review looked at 12 studies with 3474 patients to see if a procedure called PTCRA helped improve heart health. For simple heart problems, there wasn't enough evidence to show it works better than other treatments. But for more complicated heart problems, PTCRA didn't seem to help prevent blockages in arteries after a procedure called angioplasty. PTCRA might be useful in some cases where other treatments aren't possible, like for patients who can't have surgery. However, PTCRA can cause some serious side effects like spasms, perforations, and temporary blockages. Overall, there's not enough strong evidence to say PTCRA should be used routinely after angioplasty. More research is needed to know if it helps or causes more problems.

output: This review looked at one trial involving 120 families and 143 children. The trial had some problems because some families in the control group got day care services. The trial didn't show that center-based day care helped or hurt children's thinking skills or social development as measured by tests. It also didn't show that it helped or hurt how much moms worked outside the home or how much money the families made. The trial didn't look at how children did later in school or how much money they earned as adults. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say whether center-based day care is better or worse than staying at home for young children and their families in rich countries. We don't have good information to tell parents, doctors, or others what to do about day care. Some day care centers might have extra things that aren't usual, like visits from doctors. More studies comparing regular day care without extra things to regular day care might help us understand better.

output: This review looked at 15 studies involving 1098 participants. Most studies had some issues with how they were done, like not always keeping who got the treatment secret. Some studies found that getting a special medicine before getting a certain illness called CMV helped reduce the chance of getting that illness. But it didn't seem to help with another illness called acute rejection or death. When comparing the special medicine to taking medicine only when the illness happens, it seemed to work better at reducing CMV. It also caused fewer cases of a condition called leucopenia, which is when there are not enough white blood cells. However, the studies had different ways of doing things, which made it hard to know if the special medicine was really better. More studies are needed to figure out if the special medicine works better than just taking medicine when needed to prevent CMV.

output: This review looked at different ways to make a stoma (a hole in the body where waste leaves the body) after surgery for certain health problems like cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Only one study with enough information to be considered reliable was found. This study didn't find clear differences between making the stoma in a certain way (lateral pararectal) and another way (transrectal) for things like hernias, blockages, or skin irritation around the stoma. When the study looked at different types of stoma (ileostomy vs. colostomy), it also didn't find clear differences. The study didn't look at other possible problems with the stoma or if it helped or hurt the person's health. output:
This review looked at 12 studies involving 1,856 women. Most studies gave women a medicine called progestogen to help prevent miscarriages. Some studies compared progestogen to a sugar pill (placebo), while others compared it to no treatment at all. The studies came from different places like India, Jordan, the UK, and the USA. Some women had had miscarriages before, while others hadn't. The studies were mostly done well, but some weren't perfect.

When looking at all the studies together, it seems that giving progestogen might help prevent miscarriages. This is based on 10 studies that followed 1,684 women. It's not clear if this helps after having two miscarriages or three, or if it matters how the medicine is taken. The studies didn't look at other important things like how sick a woman gets during pregnancy or if she can have more babies later.

There was a small chance that progestogen might make it easier for a baby to be born alive. But the evidence for this isn't very strong. Progestogen didn't seem to affect the chances of a baby being born too early, having problems right away, or being very small. It also didn't seem to cause any extra problems for the baby.

For women who keep having miscarriages, taking progestogen might help prevent another one. More studies are needed to be sure.

output: This review looked at one study involving 72 women with sickle cell anaemia. The study wasn't perfect, so we're not sure how reliable its results are. The study didn't find any problems with having babies when women got extra blood transfusions compared to when they only got them when their health got worse. It also didn't find any clear differences in other health issues like heart trouble or breathing problems. The study did show that women who got extra blood transfusions had fewer times when they had a lot of pain. But it's hard to know if this helps because the study was small and the results aren't very clear. We don't have enough information from other studies to know if giving extra blood transfusions works better for women with different types of sickle cell disease. Right now, doctors don't have good evidence to tell them the best way to give extra blood transfusions to women with sickle cell anaemia. More research is needed to figure out the best approach.

output: This review looked at 20 studies with 2337 participants. Most studies compared a simple teaching method called brief psychoeducation with regular information given by doctors. Brief psychoeducation helped people take their medicine better in the short and medium terms (about 3 to 6 months). It also helped them stay well longer. People who got brief psychoeducation were less likely to stop taking their medicine and had fewer problems like anxiety and depression. They also seemed to do better socially and function better after a health problem. However, it didn't seem to help with overall quality of life or make people live longer. The evidence is mostly from smaller studies, so we're not sure if it works for everyone. More research is needed to know if brief psychoeducation really helps people with health problems.

output: This review looked at 10 studies with a total of 4052 women to see if adding misoprostol to other medicines helps prevent problems during childbirth. Four studies found that giving misoprostol along with other medicines didn't help reduce serious problems like death or needing to go to the ICU. Two studies compared misoprostol to oxytocin, another medicine, to see which works better. Women who got misoprostol had more bleeding than those who got oxytocin. Misoprostol can cause other side effects like vomiting and shivering. Other tests with different medicines or methods weren't done in enough women to know if they work well. The studies weren't big enough to show if misoprostol helps when used after other medicines. Oxytocin seems to be better than misoprostol for treating heavy bleeding during birth. More research is needed to find the best ways to treat women whose bleeding doesn't stop with regular medicines.

output:
This review looked at 39 studies involving 4216 participants. Out of these, 30 studies with 3392 participants had enough data to be analyzed together. Most of the studies had low or unclear risks of bias. The studies compared different solutions used to keep catheters open during dialysis (HD). Some used antibiotics, some didn't, and some used both. They looked at how often catheters got blocked (called CRI) and how often they got clotted.

Antibiotic solutions probably helped prevent CRI, but it's not clear if they made a big difference in clots. Solutions that don't have antibiotics probably didn't help much with either CRI or clots. Antibiotic and non-antibiotic solutions together seemed to work best for preventing CRI, but not for clots.

For tunnelled catheters (which stay under the skin), non-antibiotic solutions probably helped prevent CRI. But for non-tunnelled catheters (which go through the skin), they didn't seem to help much. Antibiotic solutions didn't seem to make a big difference in either CRI or clots.

Overall, using antibiotic solutions seems to help prevent blockages, but the evidence isn't strong enough to know if they help prevent clots. We need more studies to be sure about this.

output: Seven studies with 241 participants looked at different ways to lower high potassium levels in the blood, especially for people with heart problems. The studies didn't always follow the same rules, so it's hard to compare their results. Salbutamol, a medicine used to treat asthma, was found to lower potassium levels faster when given through a nebulizer (inhaled) or a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) compared to a placebo. Nebulized salbutamol worked quickly, with the biggest drop seen about an hour after taking it. Salbutamol also worked as well as insulin and dextrose, but better than bicarbonate. Other medicines like insulin and dextrose were more effective than bicarbonate and aminophylline. None of the studies looked at how well these medicines prevent serious problems. Salbutamol seems to be the best medicine to lower potassium levels quickly, but more research is needed to know if it works better than other options.

output: This review looked at 14 studies with 1298 participants to see if certain treatments helped pregnant women stop using drugs. Most studies didn't do a good job of keeping their results fair. The studies mostly looked at whether the treatments helped keep babies from being born too early or if the babies weighed less than usual. They also checked if the treatments helped keep mothers from using drugs again after giving birth. The studies found that babies stayed in the hospital for fewer days after birth when their moms got the special treatments. But the studies didn't show that the special treatments helped keep moms from using drugs again or kept babies from being born too early or weighing too little. The evidence isn't very strong because not many studies looked at these important things. More research is needed to better understand if these special treatments work for pregnant women who want to stop using drugs.

output: This review looked at 38 studies with 1828 people to see if a certain type of sugar called non-absorbable disaccharides helps prevent a condition called hepatic encephalopathy, which can happen in people with liver problems. When all the studies were looked at together, it seemed that taking this sugar might lower the chance of dying (mortality), especially when the studies were done fairly (low risk of bias). It also helped with symptoms like confusion and tiredness. The sugar didn't seem to affect the risk of serious health problems like liver failure. Taking the sugar also seemed to help with serious side effects from liver disease. The sugar didn't seem to make much difference in how well people felt overall or in how often they had minor side effects like stomach issues. Overall, the sugar might help prevent or treat hepatic encephalopathy, but more research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at 13 studies with 16,112 participants. Most studies involved people who had heart problems before. The studies found that taking a type of medicine called fibrates might help prevent some heart problems like strokes and heart attacks. When all the studies were put together, fibrates seemed to lower the chance of having a heart attack by about 16%. They didn't seem to affect how long people lived or the chance of having a stroke. Some studies showed that fibrates might help, but others didn't. This is because one type of fibrates called clofibrate was taken off the market because it had too many side effects. Without clofibrate, fibrates still seemed to help prevent heart attacks, but not strokes. The studies didn't find that fibrates caused more bad side effects. The benefits of fibrates were seen in people of different ages, genders, and those with diabetes. More studies are needed to see if fibrates work well in people who have had a stroke before and are already taking another medicine called statins.

output: This review looked at 17 studies with 1006 participants to see if psychological treatments helped reduce chest pain. The studies showed that after the treatment, people had fewer chest pain reports for the first three months, and this trend continued for up to nine months. They also had more pain-free days in the first three months. However, the benefits didn't last longer than nine months. Chest pain frequency didn't change much after the treatment. The studies found that psychological treatments, especially those using a cognitive-behavioral approach, helped reduce chest pain in the short term. Hypnotherapy might also work. But the results aren't very strong because the studies had different ways of doing things and weren't always done fairly. More research is needed to confirm these findings, especially studies that follow people for at least a year.

output: This review looked at 23 studies that tested if measuring a substance called IL-6 in the blood can help doctors diagnose sepsis in very sick adults. Most of these studies had problems that made it hard to trust their results. The studies were done in different places and with different groups of people, so it's hard to know if the findings apply everywhere. The studies also had different ways of deciding what counts as sepsis, which makes it hard to compare them. When we tried to figure out how well IL-6 works, we couldn't get clear answers because the studies were too different. Based on the information we have, IL-6 might help doctors identify sepsis, but it also means that some people who don't have sepsis might think they do, and some who do have sepsis might miss it. This is important because diagnosing sepsis quickly is crucial for treating it properly. More studies are needed to better understand how well IL-6 works and to improve the way doctors use it to diagnose sepsis.

output: This review looked at 42 studies involving 11,399 patients, including 23 new studies. Most studies showed that people who received a type of fluid called HES (hydroxyethyl starch) needed dialysis (a treatment to clean their blood) more often than those who got other fluids. HES also seemed to cause more kidney problems, like not being able to make enough urine, compared to other fluids. However, when looking at a specific way to measure kidney problems, HES didn't seem to cause more problems. The studies were generally done well, but the evidence suggests that HES increases the risk of needing dialysis and kidney problems in all types of patients. Because of these risks, doctors should use other fluids instead of HES in most cases.

output:
This review looked at 80 studies that compared different types of medicines called NSAIDs (including both regular and special kinds) with a sugar pill (placebo) or another medicine called paracetamol for treating menstrual pain. For women with primary menstrual pain, NSAIDs worked better than the placebo at reducing pain. About 45 to 53 out of every 100 women who took NSAIDs felt much better, compared to about 18 out of every 100 who took the placebo. However, NSAIDs also caused more side effects like upset stomach and headaches. About 11 to 14 out of every 100 women who took NSAIDs had side effects, compared to about 10 out of every 100 who took the placebo. 

When different types of NSAIDs were compared, there wasn't enough strong evidence to show one type was clearly better than the others. Also, there weren't enough studies comparing COX-2 specific NSAIDs to regular NSAIDs or paracetamol to see which might be safer or more effective. Most of the studies were paid for by companies, which could affect how they reported their results.

Overall, NSAIDs seem to be a good option for relieving menstrual pain, but women need to be aware that they can cause side effects. More research is needed to figure out which type of NSAID might be safest and most effective. The evidence isn't very strong because many studies didn't report their methods clearly.

output: This review looked at 11 studies with 9,839 people who had moderate to severe COPD. Most studies didn't have people who had just had a flare-up of their condition. Many of the studies were paid for by drug companies, which means they might not be completely fair. The main studies included people who weren't having a flare-up. The results show that using a medicine called LAMA plus another type of medicine (LAMA+LABA) instead of just the other medicine (LABA+ICS) helped reduce flare-ups by about 18%. It also helped people breathe better and lowered the chance of getting pneumonia. People also reported feeling better overall. However, the evidence isn't perfect because some studies had problems like not being fair or not telling us everything. So, while it seems helpful, we need more studies to be sure. This information supports new guidelines for treating COPD.

output: This review looked at four studies with 579 participants to see if an implant called ILR helps reduce long-term health problems like death. The studies didn't find clear evidence that ILR helps or hurts reducing death. They also didn't find strong evidence that it affects short-term death. Some studies suggested that ILR might help with feeling better overall and having fewer dizzy spells, but the evidence wasn't strong enough to be sure. The studies also showed that using ILR might cost more money. Overall, the evidence suggests that ILR doesn't seem to help reduce long-term death, but it might help find out the cause of the problem faster. More research is needed to see if ILR has any real benefits and to look at whether it changes things like quality of life or costs.

output: This review looked at 984 people who took part in Tai Chi exercises compared to usual care or other activities. The studies lasted from 6 weeks to a year. Most people were around 61 to 74 years old. Tai Chi helped people walk farther in 6 minutes and breathe better after the program. But it didn't seem to help with feeling short of breath or improve their quality of life much. Tai Chi didn't show clear benefits for other things like exercise ability, balance, or muscle strength. Tai Chi was safe for people with COPD. The evidence isn't strong enough to say Tai Chi helps more than usual care. When Tai Chi was added to other activities, it didn't seem to give extra benefits. More studies are needed to figure out the best way to do Tai Chi for people with COPD.

output: This review looked at seven trials involving 1697 participants. Six trials were included in the main analysis. Some of these trials had problems like not telling us everything they studied or losing some participants. The results show that latrepirdine might help improve how doctors and caregivers rate changes in someone with Alzheimer's disease after 26 weeks (CIBIC-Plus score). However, the evidence isn't strong enough to say if it helps with thinking skills (measured by ADAS-Cog and MMSE) or daily activities (measured by ADCS-ADL). There is some good-quality evidence that latrepirdine might help with behavior issues (Neuropsychiatric Inventory score). The side effects were similar in the latrepirdine group and the placebo group. Overall, the evidence suggests that latrepirdine might not improve thinking or daily activities but might help with behavior. More studies are needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at how well a medicine called PEP helps prevent HIV infection after a possible exposure. It found that getting a lot of damage to your skin during the procedure, seeing blood on the equipment, doing procedures that put a needle in the source person's blood, and if the source person has a serious illness can increase the chance of HIV spreading. However, even after adjusting for these risks, the medicine didn't seem to help stop HIV from spreading better than a placebo. Also, people who got the medicine were less likely to take it. The review suggests that healthcare workers should start taking PEP right away after a possible exposure, especially if there's a high chance of HIV spreading. But there isn't strong proof that taking more than one type of medicine works better. Healthcare workers should be told about the side effects they might have and how to deal with them. They shouldn't expect PEP to work perfectly. Since it's hard to do a big study to prove it works, healthcare workers should talk to their doctors about the best way to handle a possible HIV exposure. More research is needed to learn more about the side effects and to look at animal studies too.

output: This review looked at 22 trials involving 2193 participants who had surgery on their hands, wrists, forearms, or elbows. Most of the trials were well-designed, but some had problems keeping the groups from knowing which treatment they got. The review found that giving anesthesia through multiple injections was better than giving it in just one or two injections. This happened whether the anesthesia was given through a needle or another method. Multiple injections also helped keep the anesthesia working longer and caused less pain during the procedure. However, there wasn't enough information to know if multiple injections were safer or if they made the surgery go faster. Overall, giving anesthesia through multiple injections seems to work better, but we need more studies to be sure.

output: This review looked at 50 studies involving 45,285 participants. Most studies had some problems in how they were done, but seven studies were better at doing things correctly. These studies showed that taking statins, a type of medicine, helped prevent major health problems like heart attacks and strokes. Statins also seemed to help reduce the risk of dying from any cause. However, it's not clear if statins affect the risk of having a stroke or how well they protect kidney function. The studies didn't report on all the side effects of statins, so it's hard to know if they might cause problems like liver damage or cancer. Overall, statins seem to be helpful in preventing heart attacks and strokes in people with chronic kidney disease who haven't already had heart problems. They appear to reduce the risk of death by about 20%. More research is needed to understand the full effects of statins on kidney function and to know more about their side effects.

output: This review looked at four small studies involving 245 people who had had a stroke. The studies were mostly well done, but some had problems like not making sure who got which treatment. The studies used different ways to help people drive again, like using a driving simulator. After training, people didn't do much better on tests of their driving skills on the road. But they did do better at recognizing road signs. Using a driving simulator might help with some parts of driving, like recognizing signs, but we don't know if it helps overall driving skills. There's not enough information to say if driving training helps after a stroke or which type of training works best. More research is needed to understand what helps people drive safely after having a stroke.

output: This review looked at 11 studies with 855 participants. Nine of these studies added extra steps to a procedure called the Epley manoeuvre, which helps with a condition called Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). Adding these extra steps seemed to help more people get better from vertigo, especially when they couldn't turn their head easily. About 89 out of every 100 people who got the extra steps had their vertigo go away, compared to about 78 out of every 100 who didn't get the extra steps. This means the extra steps might make the treatment work a little bit better. But even without the extra steps, about 80 out of every 100 people still got better. The extra steps don't cause any serious problems, but they might make it a bit harder to sleep. If you have vertigo, your doctor might suggest the extra steps, but if you're uncomfortable with them, you might just do the regular Epley manoeuvre. The extra steps aren't proven to be better than the regular Epley manoeuvre, so your doctor might choose the regular one instead. More studies are needed to confirm whether the extra steps really help.

output: This review looked at six studies involving 204 premature babies. The studies found that giving extra protein in the babies' milk helped them grow faster in the hospital, especially in terms of weight, length, and head size. Babies who got extra protein stayed in the hospital a little longer and had slightly higher levels of a waste product in their blood. There wasn't enough information to know if this extra protein caused more problems like trouble eating or a condition called necrotizing enterocolitis. The studies didn't have enough babies to tell if the extra protein affected long-term growth or other health outcomes. The results might not apply to babies in less developed areas where resources are limited. More research is needed to see if giving more protein in baby formula helps with staying in the hospital longer, if it causes problems, and if it affects the babies' growth and development later on.

output: This review looked at how parents feel about getting vaccines for their children. Most parents want more information about vaccines than they get, and lack of information can make them worried or regretful about vaccinating their kids. They prefer balanced information that explains both the good and bad parts of vaccines, presented simply and tailored to their situation. Parents want vaccination information in more places, like outside of regular health services, and they want it before each visit. Health workers are important sources of information, but parents expect them to communicate well. Sometimes, poor communication or bad relationships with health workers can affect vaccination decisions. Parents often struggle to trust different sources of information and find it hard to get unbiased advice. Generally, parents who are less sure about vaccines want more information. The review found that most programs tried to improve one or two ways of communicating about vaccines, like giving information before appointments and tailoring it to parents. But they didn't address negative news stories or how parents think about why health workers do things. To help more parents feel comfortable with vaccines, planners should think about when to give information, where to find it, how to present it clearly and fairly, and how parents see health workers. More research is needed, especially in areas with fewer resources.

output:
This review looked at eight studies that tested whether a screening test for breast cancer helps save lives. Some studies found that screening didn't reduce breast cancer deaths, while others suggested it might lower them a little bit. But the studies with better ways of picking who gets screened sometimes didn't find any benefit. 

Screening led to more surgeries, like removing part of the breast (lumpectomy) or the whole breast (mastectomy), but not more chemotherapy. About 200 extra women might get treated unnecessarily, and more than 200 might feel worried about their health. 

The leaflet we made explains the pros and cons of screening so people can make a decision. Since new treatments have come out and more people know about breast cancer, the benefits of screening might be smaller now. Studies done recently show more women might be overdiagnosed and less advanced cancer might be found. So, while screening might still be helpful, it's not as clear-cut as it once was.

output: This review looked at four studies that compared using a steroid medicine on the eye with not using it for bacterial eye infections called keratitis. The studies involved a total of about 612 people. None of the studies found that using the steroid medicine made a big difference in how well people could see or in how much the infection healed. One study found that people who didn't use the steroid medicine healed faster. But another large study didn't find this difference. None of the studies found that using the steroid medicine caused more problems. Some studies lost track of some people, which might have affected the results. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say whether using the steroid medicine helps or hurts in treating bacterial eye infections. More studies with better designs are needed to get clearer answers.

output: Three small studies looked at using intramedullary nailing versus plating for fractures in the lower leg. The studies had some problems that made it hard to trust their results. The studies didn't find clear differences in how well patients did, like walking or feeling pain. Nailing seemed to lead to fewer surgeries for problems later, but the studies weren't big enough to be sure. The studies also didn't show a clear difference in how often the bones healed properly. Because the studies had limitations and were small, we're not sure if one method is better than the other. More studies are needed to help decide which method might work best for these types of fractures in adults.

output:
This review looked at 15 studies with 1835 cancer patients to see if certain treatments helped people return to work (RTW) or improve their quality of life. Most of the studies were about breast or prostate cancer. Some studies taught patients about their condition and helped them take care of themselves, while others gave patients exercise programs or made changes to their treatment plans. The studies found that:

- Teaching patients about their condition and helping them take care of themselves didn't seem to help them return to work better than usual care.
- A physical training program for breast cancer patients didn't help them return to work more than usual care.
- Less aggressive treatment for breast or prostate cancer patients didn't make it easier for them to return to work compared to more aggressive treatment.
- Combining different types of help like counseling, education, and exercise didn't seem to help patients return to work more than usual care.
- This type of combined help did seem to help patients return to work more often than usual care.

Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say these treatments definitely help patients return to work or improve their quality of life. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at how doctors ask patients about side effects after taking medicine. It found that asking patients more specifically about their symptoms led to more side effects being reported. Some side effects were reported only when patients were asked more thoroughly. However, it's not clear if this affects whether the side effects are big enough to matter. The review suggests that how doctors ask questions can affect what side effects are reported. Using more detailed questions might lead to fewer important side effects being missed. But it's not clear if this changes what kind of side effects are reported. The review had some limitations because the studies used different ways to ask questions. To get clearer results, future studies should use clear definitions for side effects and report how they were measured. They should also make sure the way they ask questions is easy for both doctors and patients to do.
