output: This review looked at 12 studies involving 3259 patients with type 2 diabetes. The studies compared regular blood sugar checks (SMBG) with usual care that didn't include checking blood sugar. Some studies checked blood sugar daily, others weekly. Most studies were done fairly well. For patients with diabetes for at least a year, regular blood sugar checks seemed to lower their blood sugar levels a little bit, but not much. After 12 months, this effect went away. Checking blood sugar didn't seem to improve how patients felt or their overall health. Two studies looked at costs and found that checking blood sugar daily cost more money than checking it less often. Few studies looked at other important things like how often patients dropped their blood sugar too low (hypoglycemia) or if it helped prevent problems like eye or kidney damage. Overall, regular blood sugar checks might help a little bit in the short term, but not much longer. Checking blood sugar doesn't seem to make patients feel better or have better overall health. More research is needed to understand the effects of regular blood sugar checks on mental health and other important aspects of living with diabetes.

This review looked at 12 studies with 3571 adults who had a lung infection called VAP. The studies compared different medicines to see which worked best. Some studies didn't tell us everything about their results, and some got money from medicine companies. 

For all-cause death, there wasn't much difference between taking just one medicine or a mix of medicines. The studies weren't sure if taking extra medicines helped or hurt. 

For getting better, there wasn't enough clear evidence to say one way was better. Some studies said taking extra medicines might help, but it's not very strong evidence. 

For staying in the hospital longer, there wasn't enough clear evidence to say one way was better. 

Some studies said taking extra medicines might cause more side effects, but it's not very strong evidence. 

One study found that a mix of tigecycline and imipenem-cilastatin seemed to make people get better more often than just tigecycline alone. But this might be because of just one study. 

Carbapenems, a type of medicine, seemed to make people get better more often, especially when looking at all patients. But it wasn't clear if this happened because of the medicine itself or because it was used in studies where patients were sicker. 

Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say which medicine is best for everyone. The review suggests that carbapenems might work better, but more studies are needed to know for sure.

This review looked at 133 studies involving 844,206 people to see how well different tests work to predict if someone might have trouble breathing through their nose or mouth or having trouble getting a tube down their throat. The tests include things like how open your mouth is, how far you can stick your tongue out, and how easy it is to see your voice box. Most of the studies were done well, but some weren't clear about how they picked who got the test and who didn't. 

For predicting trouble breathing through the nose or mouth, the upper lip bite test was the best at finding people who would have trouble, but it wasn't very good at making sure everyone else wouldn't have trouble. For predicting trouble getting a tube down the throat, the modified Mallampati test was the best at finding people who would have trouble, but it wasn't very good at making sure everyone else wouldn't have trouble.

These tests are not very good at finding people who will have trouble, but they are pretty good at making sure people don't have trouble. This means they aren't good at checking if someone might have trouble, but they are good at checking if someone definitely won't have trouble. More research is needed to create better tests that are better at finding people who might have trouble.

This review looked at 13 studies with 662 participants to see if a type of light therapy called NB-UVB worked better than other treatments for skin conditions like psoriasis and vitiligo. The studies didn't always agree on whether NB-UVB was better. Here's what we know:

- For psoriasis, one study didn't show NB-UVB was better than another treatment.
- In three studies, NB-UVB wasn't better at making the skin clear for people with psoriasis patches on both sides of their body.
- In one study, people who got NB-UVB had fewer side effects than those who got another treatment.
- For vitiligo, the studies weren't consistent about whether NB-UVB was better.
- When comparing NB-UVB to a treatment called bath PUVA, the results were mixed.
- For people with psoriasis plaques (CPP), one study found no difference between NB-UVB and topical PUVA.
- Another study found that combining NB-UVB with a medicine called retinoid worked as well as using PUVA with retinoid.
- One study found that NB-UVB was similar to a type of UVB called selective BB-UVB for clearing psoriasis plaques.
- One study found no difference between NB-UVB and topical PUVA for clearing vitiligo patches (PPP).

Overall, the results are confusing and not very strong. More studies are needed to understand if NB-UVB is helpful for these conditions. It might be easier to use than other treatments, but we need more research to know if it's safe and effective.

output: This review looked at studies comparing regular catheters with catheters treated with medicine to prevent infections. It included 57 studies with 16,784 catheters. Most studies were done well, but some couldn't hide which catheters were being tested because they looked different. The review found that treating catheters with medicine helped prevent two out of every hundred catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSIs), which is a good thing. It also helped stop bacteria growing on the catheters, which is another positive. But it didn't seem to help prevent serious sickness or death. Treating catheters with medicine didn't make much difference in preventing infections in different types of hospitals or among people getting long-term nutrition through their veins. The medicine didn't cause many side effects. So, while it helps prevent some infections, we don't have strong evidence that it saves lives or prevents serious sickness. More studies are needed to confirm these findings and see if it works in all types of hospitals and for everyone who needs a catheter.

output: This review looked at 29 studies with 5718 participants to see if using different dressings for wounds after surgery helps prevent infections. Most studies had some problems being fair in their testing. The studies mostly compared dressings like films, hydrocolloid, and silver ones with no dressings at all. They found it's not clear if using any dressing or just leaving a wound uncovered helps prevent infections. The certainty of these findings is low because the studies were small and had some flaws. There wasn't enough good information to say which type of dressing works best for preventing infections or other things like scarring or pain. So, it's hard to know if using a specific dressing will help or hurt. Because of this, doctors might choose dressings based on cost and what the patient prefers.

This review includes only one trial with 212 participants who had spinal cord injuries and severe pressure ulcers. Most participants were men. The trial compared a medicine called oxandrolone with a placebo (a fake treatment). At the end of 24 weeks, there was not enough clear evidence to say if oxandrolone helps or hurts the healing of pressure ulcers. The certainty of this evidence is very low because the results were not very precise and the participants were mostly men with spinal cord injuries.

There was also not enough clear evidence to say if oxandrolone causes more or fewer problems like feeling sick or getting sicker. The certainty of this evidence is also very low for the same reasons.

The trial stopped early because it seemed oxandrolone didn't help heal ulcers better than the placebo. Overall, there isn't strong evidence to support using oxandrolone to treat pressure ulcers. More well-designed trials are needed to see if oxandrolone works and to make sure the results are reliable.

output: This review looked at 8 studies with 580 participants to see if certain treatments help fix blocked dialysis catheters. Most studies had problems that made their results less reliable. One study found that a medicine called thrombolytic therapy might help clear the blockage, but the evidence isn't strong because it's based on just one study. Another study found that breaking open the blockage using special tools works as well as the medicine. Using tools to break open the blockage seems to keep the catheter working longer than using the medicine. But there's not enough information to know if one method is better than another for keeping the catheter clear or for how well it works during dialysis. The studies also didn't look at whether one method causes more problems. More research is needed to find out which method is best for fixing blocked catheters quickly and safely.

output: This review looked at studies about movies and commercials that show alcohol to see if they affect how much young men drink. One small study found that men who watched movies with less alcohol in them drank less than those who watched movies with more alcohol. Another study found that men who saw ads without alcohol messages drank less than those who saw ads with alcohol messages. But these studies don't have strong evidence because they might not be fair or accurate. Other studies looked at what happened when rules about showing alcohol ads changed. Some found that when rules were lifted, people bought more alcohol, especially beer and spirits. But the studies didn't look at everything that might happen, like if people got hurt or if businesses lost money. The studies also weren't funded by the alcohol companies, which means they might be honest. Right now, we don't have enough good information to know if changing alcohol ads helps or hurts drinking. We need more studies done carefully to learn more.

output: This review looked at 12 studies with 1932 patients to see if using glue instead of stitches during surgery helped reduce pain after the operation. When comparing both methods, patients who got glue had about 37% less chronic pain (pain that lasts a long time) compared to those who got stitches. However, this difference wasn't always clear because different types of mesh were used in the studies. Using lightweight mesh didn't seem to help much with pain, but using heavyweight mesh did help reduce pain. The glue method also made the operation shorter and helped patients recover faster. There were fewer problems like bleeding and swelling with the glue method. But there were no big differences in how often patients got infections or had other issues. The glue method didn't seem to make it harder for patients to get back to normal activities. The studies weren't perfect, so we're not completely sure if glue is better. More research is needed to confirm these findings and to see if the type of glue matters.

output: This review looked at 11 studies with 414 people to see if one type of therapeutic ultrasound was better than others for treating carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). The studies had mixed results, and some weren't done very well. Two studies found that ultrasound might help people feel better in the short term, but the results weren't always clear because some people didn't finish the studies. Other studies found that adding ultrasound to splints or other treatments didn't seem to work better. The studies mostly showed that ultrasound didn't make much difference in how people felt or functioned. No one got worse side effects from ultrasound. While ultrasound might help some people feel better quickly, the evidence isn't strong enough to say it works better than other treatments like splints or exercises. We need more studies to know if ultrasound is safe and effective for CTS.

output: This review looked at ten studies involving 3340 people. Some studies compared aripiprazole alone to a placebo, while others compared it to other medicines like lithium or haloperidol. Most studies lost some participants, which might affect the results. Aripiprazole helped reduce symptoms of mania in both adults and children/teens after three and four weeks, but not after six weeks. When compared to other medicines, aripiprazole didn't show better results in reducing mania symptoms. Aripiprazole caused more movement problems, like shaky hands, compared to a placebo. It also caused more stomach issues like nausea and constipation, and sometimes lowered a child's or teen's milk-making hormone levels. The studies had some differences that made it hard to compare all the results. By 12 weeks, aripiprazole didn't cause more movement problems than lithium, but it still caused more movement problems than haloperidol. Overall, aripiprazole seems to help with mania symptoms, but it has some side effects that people need to consider. More studies comparing it to other medicines are needed to know where it fits best in treatment.

output:
This review looked at two studies that compared different medicines called COX-2 inhibitors to a placebo (a pretend medicine) in people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) who also had arthritis. The COX-2 inhibitors studied were rofecoxib, valdecoxib, and lumiracoxib, but these medicines were taken off the market because of safety concerns. 

Two studies were included in the review. One study compared a medicine called etoricoxib to a placebo in people with IBD who had either ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. Another study compared another medicine called celecoxib to a placebo in people with ulcerative colitis. Both studies found that the medicines did not cause more flare-ups of IBD compared to the placebo. However, the studies were small and didn't last long enough to know if the medicines might cause other problems.

Neither study reported on side effects like stomach problems or heart issues. The studies did show that about 1 in 5 people taking the medicines had some stomach problems, but this wasn't enough to know if the medicines caused these problems. The studies also didn't find any serious side effects like death or heart problems.

Because the studies were small and didn't last long, we don't have enough information to say if these medicines are safe or not. More studies are needed to better understand the risks and benefits of these medicines in people with IBD who also have arthritis.

output: This review looked at different ways to keep people in medical studies longer. It found that giving people money to fill out surveys was helpful. Giving £20 instead of £10 worked even better. Also, offering money made people more likely to fill out surveys. Smaller surveys were not always better, and surveys about the disease helped too. Sending surveys by regular mail was better than calling people. Putting together a package of letters and reminders worked well. Having a study where people knew they were part of it worked better than a secret study. Other ideas like free stuff or special letters didn't seem to help much. We need more studies to see if these work in different situations. Money seems to be a good way to get people to stay in studies, but we need more research to know for sure.

This review looked at five studies comparing crowns to fillings in people with tooth problems. Four studies used permanent metal crowns (PMCs), and two used crowns made with a special technique called the Hall Technique. The studies found that crowns were better than fillings in the long run. Here’s what they found:

- Crowns were less likely to fail or cause pain compared to fillings.
- Crowns caused less discomfort during the procedure, especially when made using the Hall Technique.
- There was some uncertainty about whether crowns caused more bleeding around the gums compared to fillings, but the evidence wasn’t strong enough to say for sure.

Crowns were also compared to not doing anything to treat the tooth problem. This comparison didn’t have enough good-quality evidence to draw clear conclusions.

Overall, crowns seem to be a better choice than fillings for long-term protection of teeth, reducing the risk of problems like failing or causing pain. Using the Hall Technique might make the procedure less painful. But there isn’t enough good-quality evidence to say if crowns are better than not treating the tooth, or if metal crowns are better than ones with a shiny outer layer. More studies are needed to get clearer answers.

output:
This review looked at 76 studies where doctors gave a type of medicine called hyaluronan (also known as hylan) to people with knee osteoarthritis (OA) to see if it helped. Most of the studies had a good design, but some didn't follow patients for very long. The studies compared hyaluronan to nothing (placebo), other medicines, or different types of hyaluronan.

Overall, hyaluronan seemed to help reduce pain and improve how well people could move their knees. This happened most clearly in the first 5 to 13 weeks after taking the medicine. Hyaluronan worked about as well as some other medicines like ibuprofen, but lasted longer than another medicine called corticosteroids.

Most side effects were mild and went away quickly. Some studies showed that hyaluronan might work better than other medicines for knee pain, especially in the first few months after taking it. 

However, the studies weren't perfect. Different types of hyaluronan might work differently, and some studies didn't compare all the same things. So while hyaluronan seems helpful, more research is needed to know exactly how it works and if it's safe for everyone. Overall, hyaluronan appears to be a good option for treating knee OA, but it's important to talk to a doctor about the best choice for each person.

output: This review looked at five studies with a total of 149 participants. Some studies had problems keeping their results fair, so we can't be sure they were accurate. Budesonide, a medicine that helps reduce inflammation, worked better than a sugar pill for making symptoms go away and for changes seen under a microscope in the intestines. About 8 out of 10 people who took budesonide felt better compared to about 4 out of 10 who took a sugar pill. Mesalazine, a medicine often used for gut problems, didn't seem to work better when taken with another medicine called cholestyramine. Bismuth subsalicylate, a common over-the-counter medicine, didn't help more than a sugar pill for people with gut problems. Beclometasone dipropionate, another anti-inflammatory medicine, didn't seem to help more than mesalazine for people with gut problems. The studies had different results, and more research is needed to know if these medicines really work. Some people taking budesonide had stomach upset, but the studies weren't big enough to tell if this happened often. More research is needed to confirm if these medicines are helpful for people with gut problems.

output: This review looked at seven studies that had a low risk of bias. However, because the studies didn't keep everyone guessing about who got which treatment, the results might not be completely reliable. The studies showed that exercise helped reduce pain and improve physical function in people with hip osteoarthritis (OA). After the exercise ended, these benefits lasted for at least three to six months. On a scale where 0 means no pain or loss of function, exercise reduced pain by about 8 points and improved physical function by about 7 points. While exercise helped, it didn't seem to improve quality of life much. Some people felt a bit more pain during the exercise, but this wasn't a big problem. Overall, the evidence suggests that regular exercise can help people with hip OA feel less pain and have better movement. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

output:
This review looked at four small studies that involved 275 patients with hydroceles. The studies compared aspiration and sclerotherapy (injecting medicine into the hydrocele) with surgery. All studies were considered to have low or unclear risks of bias. The studies couldn't hide which treatment patients got, and it wasn't clear if the people doing the studies knew which treatment was given. 

When looking at whether the treatments worked better, the studies showed that surgery didn't do much better than aspiration and sclerotherapy. But there was a lot of difference between the studies, so we're not sure which treatment is best. 

Sclerotherapy (the medicine injection) seemed to cause more problems coming back later. Surgery caused more infections, but not enough to be sure it was different. The studies weren't able to compare how much pain people had after each treatment.

output: This review looked at 19 studies involving 3480 people with brain injuries. Most of the studies were well-designed, but some were not. For people with milder brain injuries, getting good information helps them recover well without needing extra special treatments. For those with more severe injuries, getting formal help works better, and starting rehab early usually leads to better results. People in rehab for moderate to severe injuries who get more intense treatment tend to improve faster. A special type of rehab called milieu-oriented, where patients do rehab in a supportive environment with peers, seems to work well for those with severe injuries. But it's hard to test these ideas in all cases because some people might need special care that isn't easily replaced. Different people have different problems after a brain injury, so they need different kinds of help. People with mild injuries should follow up and get advice. Those with moderate to severe injuries should have regular check-ups to plan their rehab. More intense rehab early on seems to help, but we don't know if it's worth the extra cost. Patients who finish inpatient rehab should have access to outpatient or community-based services. Group-based rehab in a supportive environment helps people with severe brain injuries. Some questions about rehab can't be answered by experiments, like which treatments work best for everyone over time. Future research will need to look at real-world data from ongoing care to answer these questions.

output:
This review looked at 35 studies from different parts of the world, mostly in high-income countries. The studies explored how people liked digital health programs, like getting reminders for medicine or appointments. Some people said these programs made them feel supported and helped them connect with others. But many people had problems using these programs. They couldn't always get cell networks or internet, or didn't have phones. Sometimes their phones were taken away by others. The cost of messages was also a big issue, and many people wanted them to be free. Language and phone skills were another problem. People were worried about privacy when it came to health topics like HIV or family planning. To solve these problems, some people suggested using simple language, sending messages at good times, and choosing the right way to deliver the messages. 

Overall, the evidence suggests that digital health programs can help with feelings of support and connection, but there are many challenges to making them work well. Program planners need to think about these challenges when creating programs. Future studies should try to fix these problems and tell us how they did so.

output: This review looked at 83 studies, but only 5 were included because they compared laser treatment to no treatment. These studies involved 4786 people with diabetes who had retinopathy. Laser treatment helped reduce the risk of losing vision by about half after 12 months (though this wasn't true for everyone). It also helped prevent severe vision loss and slowed down the progression of retinopathy. However, the studies weren't perfect because they didn't have a fair comparison group. The benefits were mostly seen in people with a more advanced form of retinopathy. The evidence isn't very strong because the studies are old and newer treatments might be better. More research is needed to see if combining laser treatment with newer treatments like anti-VEGFs could work even better.

output: This review looked at seven studies involving 349 participants with urinary catheters. Most studies had some problems in how they were done, making it hard to trust the results fully. The studies mostly looked at whether using different liquids to clean out the catheter (washouts) helps prevent infections or makes the catheter last longer. Some studies compared different types of washouts, like using salt water or acidic solutions, but the results weren't clear. The studies didn't look at things like how many times the catheter was used or how well patients liked using the washouts. Because the studies had some flaws, we can't be sure if washouts help or hurt. We need more well-designed studies to find out if washouts are helpful or harmful.

output: This review looked at 13 small studies and 3 ongoing ones that tested tai chi for heart health. Most studies had problems being sure if they were fair, and some didn't report everything clearly. The studies mostly involved healthy people, but some included those with high blood pressure, older adults at risk of falls, or those with certain types of heart trouble. Few studies looked at serious heart problems like death or major health issues. Blood pressure and cholesterol levels were measured in many studies, but the results weren't always clear. Some studies found that tai chi helped lower blood pressure and cholesterol, while others found no difference or even a small increase. One study found that tai chi improved quality of life after three months. But none of the studies looked at whether tai chi affects the risk of heart disease or diabetes. Because the studies were small and had some flaws, we don't have enough strong evidence to say tai chi helps prevent heart disease. More and better studies are needed to learn more about tai chi's effects on heart health.

output:
This review looked at 66 studies from 1988 to 2012 that studied how well endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) works in finding different stages of stomach cancer. EUS is a tool doctors use to see inside the stomach. The studies were mostly done well, but some had small problems. 

For EUS to tell if cancer has spread deep into the stomach wall (T3-T4), it was very good at doing so. It correctly identified these cancers 86 out of 100 times. For cancers that have grown into the muscle layer (T1-T2), it was even better, correct 90 out of 100 times. 

When trying to find cancers that have just reached the surface (T1a) or are growing deeper (T1b), EUS was still quite good, correct 87 out of 100 times. But for cancers that have spread to nearby lymph nodes (N-stage), it wasn't as good, correct 83 out of 100 times.

Overall, EUS helps doctors know more about where stomach cancer is located, which is helpful. But the results vary a lot between studies, so we can't be sure it's always accurate. Also, it's not as good at telling if a cancer is just on the surface or has grown deeper, or if lymph nodes have cancer. More research is needed to understand why the results differ so much.

output: A study with 46 people who have sickle cell disease found that those taking vitamin D3 had higher levels of a vitamin D chemical in their blood compared to those taking a sugar pill. Vitamin D3 helped increase vitamin D levels by about 29.79 units after eight weeks, 12.67 units after sixteen weeks, and 15.52 units after twenty-four weeks. This suggests vitamin D might help improve vitamin D levels in people with sickle cell disease. However, the study had some problems, like not having enough people finish the full six months of the study. There were no major side effects reported, but the evidence for this is not very strong. The study also looked at how much pain people had, and those taking vitamin D had less pain days, but again, the evidence is not very strong. The study didn't look at how well people felt overall, but those taking vitamin D had worse health-related quality of life scores, especially after sixteen and twenty-four weeks. Because this is just one study with some issues, it's not enough to make doctors give vitamin D to everyone with sickle cell disease. Doctors should use existing guidelines and advice about vitamin D supplements. More high-quality studies are needed to know if vitamin D helps and is safe for people with sickle cell disease.

output:
This review looked at three studies that treated children with a condition called neuroblastoma. The studies compared two types of treatment: myeloablative therapy (a strong treatment that destroys bone marrow) and conventional chemotherapy. The studies found that myeloablative therapy might help children live longer without their cancer coming back (event-free survival), but it didn't seem to give them a better chance of surviving for a longer time (overall survival) after the initial treatment. 

When researchers looked at more information from one of the studies, they still saw that myeloablative therapy helped prevent the cancer from coming back. But they couldn't find enough information to say if it helped children live longer overall.

The studies didn't find any clear differences in serious side effects like infections or kidney problems. However, they did see more of these side effects in the group that got myeloablative therapy.

The studies also didn't look at how well the children felt or how their lives were affected by the treatments. Some of the studies had problems that might make the results less reliable.

Based on what we know now, myeloablative therapy might help prevent the cancer from coming back, but it's not clear if it helps children live longer. More research is needed to figure out the best way to treat this condition, especially since the definition of "high-risk" has changed. Future studies should be done carefully to make sure they're comparing apples to apples and follow patients for a long time to get a clearer picture.

output: This review looked at nine studies involving 1512 women who were trying to get pregnant. Most studies involved women who were having fertility treatments like IUI (intrauterine insemination). The studies mostly compared a procedure called intentional endometrial injury, where the lining of the uterus is slightly damaged, to no damage or a fake procedure. The results are not very clear if this procedure helps women get pregnant or have a baby. Some studies suggested it might help, but the evidence isn't strong enough to be sure. The studies showed that the procedure might make it easier for some women to get pregnant, but the evidence for this is also not very good. The pain during the procedure was usually not very bad, around a 6 out of 10. But only one study reported this. The timing of the procedure didn't seem to matter much. The studies didn't find any evidence that this procedure increases the risk of miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or twins. Overall, we're not sure if this procedure helps women get pregnant or have a baby. More studies are needed to know for sure.

output: This review looked at 42 studies with 4220 participants to see how well a type of ultrasound called CDUS and another called CE-CDUS work in detecting a condition called endoleak. Most of the studies were not very good because it was hard to know if the doctors were blind to the results or if they knew which test was done first. The studies that used CDUS found that the test was about 82% accurate for picking up endoleaks and 93% accurate for ruling them out. The studies that used CE-CDUS found it was 94% accurate for picking up endoleaks and 95% accurate for ruling them out. Using contrast made the CDUS test much better at finding endoleaks. The studies that used CE-CDUS were better done than those that used CDUS. The studies that used CDUS got better results before 2006 compared to those that used it after 2006. When looking at the studies that used scans instead of individual participants, the results were similar. Overall, CE-CDUS seems to be better at finding endoleaks than CDUS. So, for checking endoleaks, using CE-CDUS might be a good choice first, followed by a CT scan if the ultrasound is positive.

output: This review looked at 25 studies involving 3663 children. Most studies were done well and fairly. The results show that children who took oral antibiotics were more likely to have their ear infections go away completely after two to three months compared to those who didn't take antibiotics (2 out of every 5 children benefited). But, they were also more likely to get side effects like diarrhea, vomiting, or a rash (about 20 children would need to take antibiotics for one child to get these side effects). Antibiotics seemed to help children's ears heal faster, but it wasn't clear if they helped hearing. Antibiotics didn't seem to cause more problems like needing tubes in the ears or having more ear infections later. However, the benefits of antibiotics for ear infections might not last as long as we thought. It's important to weigh the good and bad effects of antibiotics and consider whether they're really necessary for treating ear infections.

This review looked at 40 new studies and 7 ongoing ones. It included 63 studies in total, focusing on regional anesthesia to prevent pain problems (PPP) after surgeries. The studies showed that:

- For surgeries like thoracotomies, using epidural anesthesia might help reduce PPP for up to 18 months (odds ratio [OR] 0.52, meaning it's about half as likely to happen).
- For breast cancer surgeries, regional anesthesia might help reduce PPP for up to 12 months (OR 0.43).
- For cesarean sections, regional anesthesia might help reduce PPP for up to 8 months (OR 0.46).

However, the evidence isn't strong enough to say if other types of surgeries or different anesthesia methods work. The studies had some flaws, so we're not completely sure about the results. More and better studies are needed to make stronger conclusions.

output: This review looked at four studies involving 231 people. Most of the studies didn't follow good methods, so we can't be sure their results are accurate. The studies compared different surgeries and treatments like steroids and antibiotics for a condition called chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Some studies found that surgeries and medicines worked about the same for reducing symptoms and improving quality of life. Other studies showed that surgeries might help a bit more in one area, but it wasn't clear if this made much difference. The studies also found that both surgeries and medicines had similar side effects, like nosebleeds. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say one treatment is clearly better than another. More research is needed to understand which treatments work best and if they improve quality of life or reduce healthcare costs.

output:
This review looked at six studies with a total of 137 people to see if a treatment called tDCS helps with Parkinson's disease. The studies mostly compared tDCS to a fake treatment (called sham tDCS). Here’s what they found:

- tDCS didn't seem to help with overall symptoms of Parkinson's (like how well someone can move).
- tDCS did seem to help with specific parts of movement, like how fast someone can walk.
- tDCS didn't help with how much time someone spends without symptoms (off time) or with involuntary movements (on time).
- tDCS didn't improve how well people do everyday tasks.
- tDCS didn't seem to make health-related quality of life better.
- tDCS didn't cause more people to stop taking part in the study or have bad side effects compared to the fake treatment.

Overall, the evidence isn’t strong enough to say tDCS works well for Parkinson's disease. More studies are needed to learn more about it.

This review looked at 77 studies with 6287 participants to see if certain medicines helped people with a type of liver disease called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Most of the studies weren't done very well, so we can't be sure of their results. 

For people with NAFLD who don't have diabetes, some studies looked at different medicines. But none of the studies showed that these medicines helped people live longer or had fewer bad side effects. Some studies didn't even look at how well people felt or how healthy their livers were.

The medicines studied were antioxidants, bile acids, and thiazolidinediones. None of the studies found that these medicines made people live longer or had fewer bad side effects. 

Some studies got money from companies that might benefit from the results, while others didn't get extra money. We're not very sure if these medicines work because the studies weren't done very well. We need more studies with lots of people to know better.

output: This review looked at 18 studies involving 4843 participants to see if taking bisphosphonates helped reduce pain or other problems in people with bone issues. While bisphosphonates didn't seem to make much difference in how many people got better from pain, they did seem to help prevent something called skeletal-related events, which are bad things that happen to bones. Bisphosphonates also didn't seem to affect how long people lived. However, they caused more nausea and kidney problems. The studies weren't perfect, so we're not sure if these effects are really big or just small. Bisphosphonates might help keep the bones from getting worse, but we need more studies to confirm this. It's important to weigh the potential benefits against the side effects like nausea and kidney trouble. Future studies should use the same ways to measure how people feel to get clearer answers.

output: This study looked at a small number of women (24) who had severe pre-eclampsia. It compared a group that got special medicines and fluids to help lower blood pressure with another group that got an epidural instead. The study found that the group getting the epidural had slightly lower blood pressure, but it didn't find any difference in how the babies did. The study wasn't perfect because it had some flaws that made it hard to trust the results fully. The study didn't look at important things like if the mothers or babies had serious problems. Because the study was small and not done properly, we don't have enough good information to know if epidurals work better than other treatments for severe pre-eclampsia. We need bigger, better-controlled studies to figure out if epidurals help mothers and babies and if they're safe and worth the cost.

output: This review looked at 12 trials with 1319 participants. Most of the studies had some problems in how they were done, so we can't be completely sure of their results. The studies mostly involved people who had eye problems called glaucoma. They found that giving a medicine called 5-FU after a surgery called trabeculectomy helped reduce the chance of the surgery failing in the first year, especially for people who were at higher risk of it failing. It also helped lower the pressure inside the eye. But, using 5-FU also made some people get more eye problems. The benefits were seen mainly in people who had the surgery for the first time and were at higher risk of it failing. The number of people who needed to get the medicine to see a benefit was about 4 for high-risk people and 5 for those having their first surgery. The medicine didn't seem to help if given to people who had the surgery more than once. While the medicine helped, it also caused more eye problems. Since the medicine isn't used much anymore, it's probably because some people don't like the extra risks. More research is needed to confirm these findings and consider how important the benefits are compared to the extra risks.

output: This review looked at 58 trials where 2849 people were given a local anaesthetic injection around the belly during a laparoscopic gallbladder operation. Most of the trials were done in people with low risk of complications. The local anaesthetic injections seemed to reduce pain and make people feel better during and after the operation. However, there was no difference in how quickly people recovered or returned to normal activities. The evidence is not very strong because the trials had some flaws. It's not clear if the pain relief is big enough to matter. More trials are needed to confirm these findings and to look at other important outcomes like how well people feel and how soon they can go back to work.

output: This review looked at eight studies involving 2488 people to see if capsaicin, a compound found in chili peppers, helps with nerve pain. For people with shingles pain (postherpetic neuralgia), capsaicin worked better than a fake treatment called a placebo. About 10% more people said their pain was much or very much better after 8 or 12 weeks with capsaicin than with the placebo. For people with pain from HIV, capsaicin also seemed to work better than a placebo, though the results weren't as clear. For people with diabetes-related nerve pain, capsaicin helped about 10% more people feel better over 2 to 12 weeks. But for people who had surgery and still had pain afterward, capsaicin didn't seem to help more than a fake treatment. The evidence isn't very strong because there wasn't much data, and it's hard to know if the results are real. Some people did have side effects like feeling sick, but not many. Overall, capsaicin seems to help reduce pain, especially for shingles and HIV pain, but the benefits aren't huge. It works similarly to other pain treatments.

output:
This review looked at 26 studies that compared different ways to reduce exposure to something that might cause asthma symptoms. Some studies found that reducing exposure, like using less of a harmful substance or changing jobs, helped people feel better. Other studies found that completely removing someone from exposure to the harmful thing also helped, especially if the person was exposed to low-molecular-weight substances. 

When comparing these two approaches, removing someone from exposure seemed to help more with asthma symptoms and lung function, especially for those exposed to low-molecular-weight substances. But removing someone from exposure might also lead to more people losing their jobs. 

The evidence isn't very strong because the studies weren't always done in the best way. So, while removing someone from exposure seems to help, we need more research to know for sure. It's important for doctors and employers to consider both the good and bad effects of these changes.

output: This review looked at 23 trials with 1586 participants to see if quinine, vitamin E, or other treatments helped reduce muscle cramps. Most of the trials were not very good at making sure who got which treatment. Quinine was found to reduce the number and intensity of cramps compared to a sugar pill, but it caused more upset stomach. It didn't seem to cause more serious side effects. A mix of quinine and vitamin E didn't work better than just quinine. Adding the drug theophylline to quinine seemed to make cramps go away more. Getting injections into the calf muscle didn't help much either. Vitamin E didn't seem to help. There isn't strong enough evidence to know the best dose or length of time to take quinine. More research is needed to find out if other treatments like vitamin E or the theophylline mix are better. Larger studies would help us understand how long quinine works and if it has long-term side effects.

output: This review looked at four studies involving 1190 women who had suspected large babies. The studies found that inducing labor did not make it more likely for women to have a cesarean section or an instrument-assisted delivery. However, it did reduce the chance of needing a forceps or vacuum delivery, and it lowered the risk of shoulder problems and broken bones during birth. There was less bleeding after birth too. The studies also showed that babies born after induction weighed less on average. But the studies had some flaws, like not always keeping everyone guessing which group got the treatment. The results suggest that inducing labor for suspected large babies might help prevent some injuries, but it doesn't seem to affect the overall risk of major surgery. Some doctors think it might be helpful, but others don't. More studies are needed to confirm if inducing labor before term is really better for babies.

output: This review looked at five studies involving 1819 women who had planned early delivery compared to usual care. Women who had planned early delivery had a lower risk of having problems during their pregnancy, like HELLP syndrome and severe kidney issues. However, they were more likely to have breathing problems in their babies and spend more time in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). Planned early delivery didn't seem to affect the risk of death for the baby. Most of the evidence comes from two large, well-designed studies, but some of the results are uncertain because the studies had different ways of doing things that might have affected the results. Overall, planned early delivery seems to help reduce some problems during pregnancy, but more research is needed to know if it helps with all possible problems.

output:
This review looked at 12 studies with 799 participants to see if different types of arch wires help teeth move better or cause less pain. Here's what we found:

- For multistrand stainless steel and superelastic NiTi arch wires, we couldn't tell if one type helps teeth move faster or causes less pain. The studies weren't very good.
- For multistrand stainless steel and thermoelastic NiTi arch wires, we didn't have enough good studies to know if one type helps teeth move faster or causes less pain.
- For conventional NiTi and superelastic NiTi arch wires, we didn't have enough good studies to know if one type helps teeth move faster or causes less pain.
- For conventional NiTi and thermoelastic NiTi arch wires, we didn't have enough good studies to know if one type helps teeth move faster or causes less pain.
- For single-strand superelastic NiTi and coaxial superelastic NiTi arch wires, we found that coaxial superelastic NiTi wires helped teeth move more over 12 weeks, but we don't know if this causes less pain.
- For superelastic NiTi and thermoelastic NiTi arch wires, we didn't have enough good studies to know if one type helps teeth move faster or causes less pain.

Overall, we don't have strong evidence to say which type of arch wire is best for moving teeth or causing less pain. More good studies are needed.

output: This review looked at 19 studies with 2663 participants. Most studies focused on outpatients with milder heart failure symptoms. Antibiotics seemed to reduce the chance of treatment failing by about 20% in the first month compared to a placebo, but the evidence wasn't very strong. Some older antibiotics didn't seem to work better. Antibiotics didn't seem to lower death rates or stop more flare-ups. One study found that antibiotics might make it easier to recover from a heart attack in the ICU, but the results weren't clear for everyone else. Antibiotics didn't seem to improve overall quality of life or cause more side effects. The review suggests that antibiotics might help some people with heart failure, especially those in the ICU, but the effects aren't always consistent. More research is needed to find out who will really benefit from antibiotics and who might not.

output: This review looked at 11 studies involving 3060 people with advanced prostate cancer. The studies found that taking non-steroidal anti-androgens, which are medicines that block male hormones, did not help people live longer and made it more likely that their cancer would progress or stop working. This happened more often than when people had surgery or medicine to remove their testicles. The evidence for these findings is considered moderate, meaning it's not very strong. Non-steroidal anti-androgens also caused more side effects like breast pain, gynecomastia (enlarged breasts), and feeling tired. However, they helped reduce other side effects like hot flashes. The review suggests that non-steroidal anti-androgens are not as good as removing the testicles for treating advanced prostate cancer. More research is needed to confirm these findings, especially for people who haven't spread their cancer yet. But for those whose cancer has spread, further research might not be necessary.

output: This review looked at 15 studies involving 1282 people with memory problems (MCI) who were followed for about a year to four years. Some of these people developed Alzheimer's disease, while others developed other types of dementia. The review found that certain proteins in spinal fluid (CSF) can help tell the difference between people with MCI and those who develop Alzheimer's disease. However, the tests are not perfect and can sometimes give wrong answers. The tests for two of these proteins, tau and beta-amyloid, were fairly accurate, but the test for all three together was less so. The studies had some problems, making it hard to know if the results are reliable. Because of these issues, we don't have strong evidence to say these tests are useful for diagnosing Alzheimer's disease right now. It's important to use these tests carefully to avoid mistakes. The tests are better at telling if someone doesn't have Alzheimer's rather than if they do. More research is needed to make these tests clearer and more consistent.

output:
This review includes just one study that compared two treatments for children with a condition called Childhood Apraxia of Speech (CAS). The study involved 26 children aged 4 to 12 years who had mild to moderate CAS. The children were randomly assigned to receive either the Nuffield Dyspraxia Programme-3 (NDP-3) or the Rapid Syllable Transitions Treatment (ReST). Both treatments were given in intensive one-hour sessions, four days a week for three weeks, at a university clinic in Australia. 

The study found that both treatments helped improve the children's speech, especially in producing words correctly and speaking consistently. However, the improvements were slightly better for the NDP-3 treatment compared to ReST for some measures. But for another measure, ReST showed a slight edge. 

The study didn't look at how well the children did in real-life situations or if the treatments worked better than usual care. It also didn't compare NDP-3 and ReST directly. Because it was the only study, the results aren't very strong. More research is needed to see if these treatments work better than others or if they're better than usual care.

output: This review looked at 38 studies with 1896 participants. Only one study was done fairly and honestly. Many studies had problems with how they were set up or reported their results. Some studies looked at helping people recover after they had surgery to fix broken bones. Others looked at helping people recover after they had a splint or cast on their broken bones. The studies found that allowing people to move around a bit during the time they were in a splint or cast helped them move their feet better and feel less pain. But it also meant they might have a few small problems like feeling dizzy or queasy. Starting to put weight on the foot right away seemed to help too. Some special electrical treatments might help a little bit too. However, there isn't strong evidence that doing stretches or getting massages helps. And there's no clear answer about which type of splint or cast is best. More studies are needed to learn more about what works best for recovery after broken bones.

Nine studies looked at different gases used to create space inside the belly during surgery for heart problems. Most studies didn't follow good methods, so we can't be sure if the results are accurate. 

For gases like nitrous oxide, helium, and room air compared to carbon dioxide:

- We don't have enough clear evidence to say if these gases help prevent heart or lung problems after surgery.
- They didn't seem to cause more serious problems like breathing issues or death.
- Some studies showed that using room air instead of carbon dioxide might make people feel less pain after surgery, but this isn't very strong evidence.
- Room air seemed to cost less money to use during surgery, but we're not sure if this is true for everyone.
- We know that using helium or nitrous oxide doesn't seem to help much, and there's not enough information to say if it causes more problems.
- It's not clear if helium, nitrous oxide, or room air are safer than carbon dioxide for this type of surgery.
- More studies are needed to find out which gas works best and if it's safe for everyone who needs this kind of surgery.

output:
This review looked at 15 studies, mostly in poor areas like slums in Bangladesh, India, and Peru. It focused on giving extra vitamins and minerals to mothers and kids to help their health. The studies tried different ways to give these supplements, like zinc to mommies during pregnancy and vitamins to kids. Some studies also taught moms about healthy eating. But many of the studies had problems that made it hard to trust the results fully. 

For babies born too early (LBW), there wasn't enough good evidence to show that giving extra vitamins helped. For babies' height, some studies suggested it might help a little bit, but the evidence wasn't strong. Teaching moms about healthy eating seemed to help make babies less likely to be born too early. 

Giving extra vitamins to kids didn't seem to help much with babies being born too early or growing taller. The studies also showed that giving extra vitamins to kids might help them grow taller, but the evidence wasn't very strong.

Overall, the studies showed that giving extra vitamins could help reduce something called "stunting," which means kids aren't growing as well as they should. But the studies didn't find that the specific programs they looked at worked to reduce stunting in these areas.

This review looked at 15 studies, mostly in poor areas like slums in Bangladesh, India, and Peru. It focused on giving extra vitamins and minerals to mothers and kids to help their health. The studies tried different ways to give these supplements, like zinc to mommies during pregnancy and vitamins to kids. Some studies also taught moms about healthy eating. But many of the studies had problems that made it hard to trust the results fully. 

For babies born too early (LBW), there wasn't enough good evidence to show that giving extra vitamins helped. For babies' height, some studies suggested it might help a little bit, but the evidence wasn't strong. Teaching moms about healthy eating seemed to help make babies less likely to be born too early. 

Giving extra vitamins to kids didn't seem to help much with babies being born too early or growing taller. The studies also showed that giving extra vitamins to kids might help them grow taller, but the evidence wasn't very strong.

Overall, the studies showed that giving extra vitamins could help reduce something called "stunting," which means kids aren't growing as well as they should. But the studies didn't find that the specific programs they looked at worked to reduce stunting in these areas.

It's important to consider that living in slums can be challenging, with lots of moving around and not having many services. More research is needed to see if combining different types of programs and changes in policies can help improve nutrition in these areas.

output: This review looked at three studies involving a total of 516 participants. Two studies compared silicone oil and sulfur hexafluoride gas, and one compared silicone oil and perfluoropropane gas. For people with a condition called retinal detachment (RD) that happens with something called proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR), the studies found that using silicone oil or perfluoropropane gas didn't make much difference in how well their vision improved or if their retina attached back to their eye. Sulfur hexafluoride gas seemed to cause worse vision problems in the first year, but not in the second year. Silicone oil helped more with keeping the retina attached in both the first and second years. The studies weren't perfect, but they generally followed good practices. The choice of which gas to use might depend on what the doctor thinks is best for each person. Another type of silicone oil, which isn't commonly used in the USA, didn't show better results than regular silicone oil in the studies.

output: This review looked at three studies with a total of 492 people who had hip replacement surgery (THA). The studies had some problems in how they were done, so we're not sure about their results. One study found that giving hip precautions, equipment, and restrictions didn't seem to help people's function or quality of life better than not giving them. Another study found that people who got these precautions might feel a little bit happier about their recovery, but it wasn't clear if this was true. Both studies said there were no hip dislocations or bad side effects. The third study found that people who got extra education and rehabilitation services after surgery didn't have better function at six months than those who got regular rehabilitation. None of the studies measured pain, how well people thought the treatment worked, or how often people needed to go back to the hospital. Overall, we don't know if giving hip precautions, equipment, and restrictions helps prevent hip dislocations or improves outcomes after THA. There isn't enough good evidence to say whether having a special post-rehabilitation program in the community works better than usual care. More high-quality studies are needed to find out.

output: This review looked at studies that tried to prevent blood clots called VTE in children who have tubes in their veins (CVCs) to help with medicine. The studies used different treatments like special medicines, adding extra clot-fighting proteins, or using blood products. But the studies had some problems, and the results weren't always clear. Overall, the studies didn't show that any of these treatments worked better than doing nothing to prevent VTE. Some studies did find that adding a special medicine called LMWH to another treatment might help prevent VTE, but it didn't cause more bleeding. The studies also didn't find that any of the treatments caused other bad side effects like strokes or infections. Because there weren't many children in the studies, it's hard to know if the treatments really work. More studies are needed to learn more about these treatments and how well they work in preventing VTE in children with CVCs.

output:
This review looked at 14 studies with 2488 people who had Bell's palsy. Most of the studies were small and had some problems being fair. The main findings were:

- A mix of medicines called antivirals and corticosteroids didn't seem to help more than just corticosteroids for people with Bell's palsy.
- People who got just corticosteroids recovered better than those who got just antivirals.
- Getting both antivirals and corticosteroids might help people recover faster and less likely to have long-term problems like crocodile tears or motor synkinesis.
- The chance of having these long-term problems was lower with antivirals and corticosteroids compared to just corticosteroids.
- There wasn't much difference in bad side effects between the different groups.
- Some studies showed fewer long-term problems in people who took corticosteroids compared to those who took antivirals.
- More studies comparing different antiviral medicines might be needed to see if one works better.

Overall, the evidence suggests that getting antivirals and corticosteroids together might help with recovery and reduce long-term problems, but the results aren't very strong. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at six crossover trials and two parallel group trials that tested a treatment called SNS for a condition called fecal incontinence (FI). In one trial, 53 people with severe FI who got SNS had fewer episodes of leaking poop compared to those who got regular medicine. Some people had side effects like pain at the place where the device was put in. Another trial found similar results. In another trial, fewer people with FI had leaks when they got SNS instead of a different treatment. But in this trial, some people had mild pain. In some trials, the number of times people leaked poop changed depending on whether the SNS was turned on or off. In other trials, SNS didn't help with constipation. Overall, the evidence suggests that SNS might help some people with FI have better control over their bowels, but it doesn't seem to help with constipation. Some people had side effects like pain or infections. More high-quality trials are needed to learn more about SNS and its effects.

This review looked at 85 studies to understand what healthy pregnant and postpartum women, as well as healthcare providers, think about antenatal care (ANC). The studies came from many different countries, including rich and poor ones, in cities and villages. The researchers found 52 important points, grouped into three main areas: how things work in the community, how ANC is set up and given, and what matters most to women and healthcare workers. 

They found that women use ANC if they think it will be helpful and safe. This means having good, free services that are close by and where they feel comfortable. Women also like it if the staff are kind, caring, and respectful. 

For healthcare providers, it helps if they have enough money, time, and support to give good care. They need to be trained well and paid fairly so they don't need to ask for extra money from patients.

Overall, this review shows us what makes ANC useful or not useful. It helps us know what to improve in ANC services to make them better for everyone.

This review looked at 112 studies about heart failure treatments for people with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Most studies didn't do a good job of comparing treatments fairly. The studies mostly looked at heart failure in adults, but some included people with CKD. Here's what we know:

- For heart failure in general, some medicines like adenosine A1-receptor antagonists, dopamine, nesiritide, and serelaxin don't seem to help much or have mixed effects.
- Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) might not help or might even make things worse in some cases.
- Beta-blockers might help lower the risk of dying from heart problems.
- Aldosterone antagonists might raise the chance of having too much potassium in the blood.
- Vasopressin receptor antagonists might not affect heart failure or kidney health.
- Sinus node inhibitors haven't been studied enough to know if they affect potassium levels.
- Other treatments like digoxin, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, renin inhibitors, and vasodilators haven't been studied well enough to know their effects.

Overall, we're not sure if these treatments work well for people with both heart failure and CKD. More studies are needed to better understand how different treatments might affect people with CKD who have heart failure.

output: This review looked at seven studies involving 735 people to see if red yeast rice (RIC) helps prevent and treat strokes. Most studies were done well, but some had flaws. For people with narrowed arteries in their brain, RIC seemed to lower the chance of having another stroke. But for those having a stroke right away, RIC didn't seem to help reduce the size of the stroke or make them feel better. RIC caused more side effects, like feeling sick or dizzy, but no serious problems were reported. The studies weren't big enough or clear enough to know if RIC helps or hurts in all cases. More research is needed to understand its effects better.

output: This review looked at 10 studies that tested educational interventions to help children with atopic eczema. Most of the studies were done in regular doctor's offices. The studies showed that children who got the educational interventions had less severe eczema and felt better about their skin. The biggest study found that children who had six age-appropriate group lessons had less severe eczema and felt better overall. However, the improvements weren't always big enough to make a real difference in how children felt. The studies didn't look at whether the interventions helped prevent serious health problems. Some of the studies had flaws, like not doing a good job of making sure everyone was treated fairly. The new studies added to the review didn't change the main idea that these educational interventions might help. But the studies didn't describe exactly how they were done, so it's hard to know if they would work the same way in other places. More research is needed to see if these interventions really help and if they're worth the time and effort.

output: This review looked at 29 studies where people with asthma were given different ways to learn how to use their inhalers better. Most studies didn't have many problems, but some had issues that made it hard to know if the new ways worked well. The studies showed that teaching people how to use their inhalers correctly helped them do it better, especially right away and a few weeks later. But it wasn't always clear if these better techniques made a big difference in how well people felt or if they had fewer breathing problems. The studies also weren't always done in the same way, so it was hard to compare them all. Overall, while learning how to use inhalers better might help some people feel better, the evidence isn't strong enough to say it works for everyone. It's not clear the best way to teach people or how often to check if they're using their inhalers correctly. More research is needed to figure out the best approach.

This review looked at seven studies involving 825 people to see if certain types of help, like talking about drinking problems and doing special exercises, could reduce heavy drinking. The studies were not always done well, so we can't be sure how good the results are. Here's what we found:

- One study comparing two types of help didn't show one type worked better.
- Another study found that getting quick advice didn't help people drink less.
- Motivational interviewing, a way to encourage people to change their behavior, didn't seem to work better than usual care.
- A shorter version of motivational interviewing didn't help people drink less either.
- Intensive motivational interviewing didn't show any clear benefits either.

Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say which type of help works best. More studies are needed to find out.

This review looked at three studies involving 91 children aged 6 months to 4 years with croup. The studies used a special mix of air called heliox, which is 70% helium and 30% oxygen, to treat croup. The studies lasted from 7 to 16 months and were done in emergency rooms in the USA and Spain. 

For children with mild croup, one study found that heliox might not make their croup better faster than regular oxygen. Another study found that heliox might help children feel better faster, but it didn't last longer. The studies were not perfect, so we're not sure if heliox really helps or not. Most children got better and left the hospital, but we don't know if they stayed well or came back. 

Heliox might help children with moderate to severe croup feel better faster, especially if they get medicine to calm their breathing. But we don't know if it's safer or works better than other treatments. We need more studies to find out if heliox is helpful and safe for children with croup.

output: This review looked at 27 studies that tested different family-based programs to help kids avoid smoking. The programs varied a lot, but most involved teaching parents and kids about healthy habits together. Some studies compared families getting special programs to those who didn't get any extra help. Overall, the studies showed that family-based programs can help prevent kids from starting to smoke. When comparing families getting both family and school programs to just school programs, there was a slight chance that the family program might work better. But the evidence isn't strong enough to know for sure. The programs usually taught parents to be supportive and caring, which helped kids avoid smoking. The studies found that family-based programs could make it less likely for kids to start smoking, but the exact amount is hard to say. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at 12 studies involving 563 people with sickle cell disease, mostly African-American, aged 6 to 35 years. The studies varied in how often they met, how long they lasted, and where they took place. Most studies had low risk of bias, but some had other issues. Four studies showed that educational programs helped people with sickle cell disease learn more about their condition. This was true for both patients and caregivers, but the benefits for caregivers didn't last as long. The programs didn't seem to help people recognize signs of their illness or use more health services. However, they did help reduce depression. The programs also seemed to make patients stick to their treatment plans. While the benefits were small, the programs did seem to work better for patients than caregivers. More research is needed to confirm these findings and to see if they lead to better health outcomes.

output: This review looked at four studies involving more than 13,000 women in labor in the UK and Ireland. The studies were done fairly, and the results haven't changed since 2012. The studies found that women who had continuous electronic fetal monitoring (CTG) had a slightly higher chance of needing a cesarean section compared to those who had regular listening to the baby's heartbeat. However, there wasn't enough evidence to show that CTG helps with other problems like breathing difficulties or death of the baby after birth. Also, CTG led to more frequent use of continuous electronic fetal monitoring and fetal blood tests. The review suggests that CTG might increase the chance of a cesarean section without providing extra benefits. Since the studies didn't find strong evidence of benefit, it's recommended that doctors not use CTG for low-risk women in labor. Women should be told that CTG might lead to more cesareans without clear benefits. The information is mostly reliable, but not perfect. More studies are needed to confirm these findings, especially in places where CTG is still used.

output: This review looked at 19 studies that tested three types of amphetamines—dexamphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, and mixed amphetamine salts—to see if they help with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). About 2500 people took part in these studies. Most of the studies lasted about 5 weeks. The studies found that amphetamines helped reduce symptoms of ADHD, like trouble paying attention, as measured by doctors and patients. However, they didn't help people stay in treatment longer. Amphetamines caused more people to stop taking the medicine because of side effects. Different types of amphetamines worked differently. Lisdexamfetamine and mixed amphetamine salts seemed to work better at reducing ADHD symptoms. Dexamphetamine didn't seem to help much. The studies weren't perfect, so we can't be sure how well amphetamines work for everyone. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at 57 studies where 34,390 people were given digital interventions to help them drink less alcohol. Most of these studies had some problems in how they were done, like not keeping track of who dropped out. The studies that worked well showed that people who got digital interventions drank about 23 grams of alcohol less each week compared to those who didn't get any special help. This is about 3 UK units of alcohol, which is a small amount. People also had fewer days when they drank too much alcohol. The digital interventions seemed to work better than usual care, but it's hard to know if this is true because some studies didn't tell us if people had any bad side effects. Some things that helped people stick to their new habits, like setting goals and getting advice, seemed to make digital interventions more effective. However, there wasn't enough evidence to say if digital interventions were better than talking to someone in person. Also, not many studies talked about why the interventions worked, and even fewer used theories to design them. Overall, there's moderate-quality evidence that digital interventions can help people drink less alcohol, but more research is needed to confirm this.

output: This review looked at five studies with 240 children aged 1 to 18 years who had mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The studies were done in special sleep clinics at big hospitals. They compared different treatments like nasal steroid sprays and a medication called montelukast. The studies found that children who took montelukast had fewer breathing problems during sleep compared to those who took a placebo. However, the studies weren't perfect and it's hard to know if the benefits are really strong. The nasal steroid sprays didn't seem to help much. Some children had minor side effects like nosebleeds, but these were rare. Montelukast seemed to improve how well children breathed and how often they woke up during sleep. But the studies couldn't tell if these changes were big enough to matter. It's not clear if these treatments work better than surgery for OSA. More studies are needed to see if these treatments are safe and effective in the long run, especially for things like attention and school performance.

output: This review looked at 28 studies involving 788 children and adults who used different techniques to clear their lungs, like Positive Expiratory Pressure (PEP). Most studies didn't show a big difference in how well PEP worked compared to other methods for clearing the lungs, especially when looking at how much air they could blow out quickly (forced expiratory volume in one second). But longer studies sometimes showed PEP might help reduce coughing fits (respiratory exacerbations) over time. PEP was also preferred by most people who tried it. PEP was linked to fewer coughing fits when used with a mask for at least a year. Some studies found PEP might cause less irritation in the lower airways compared to another method called High-Frequency Chest Wall Oscillation (HFCWO). However, there wasn't enough good-quality information about other possible side effects. The studies varied in how well they were done, so the results aren't perfect. Overall, PEP seems to be helpful for reducing coughing fits, but it's best to use it as part of a plan that fits each person's needs.

This review looked at 7524 people who took part in 40 studies comparing a treatment called Intensive Case Management (ICM) with regular care or another type of care. Most studies had some problems in how they were done, so we can't be sure about the results. 

When ICM was compared to regular care, it seemed to help people stay out of the hospital for shorter periods of time and keep going with their treatment. It also helped people leave the study less often. But it didn't seem to help people stay out of the hospital longer or have fewer bad things happen to them. 

When ICM was compared to another type of care, it didn't seem to help people stay out of the hospital for longer periods or have fewer bad things happen to them. It also didn't seem to help people get back to work more easily. 

Studies found that if ICM followed the rules of the ACT model (a way of helping people with mental health issues) more closely, it worked better at keeping people out of the hospital. But it's not clear if ICM helps more than just following the rules of the ACT model. 

Overall, ICM seems to help people with mental health issues by keeping them out of the hospital and staying in treatment longer. But we don't know if it helps them feel better or have a better quality of life. More studies are needed to find out if ICM works better than other types of care.

This review looked at 67 studies involving 6197 people. Most of these studies had problems in how they were done, so we can't be sure their results are accurate. Only one study showed a clear difference: using a radiofrequency dissecting sealer led to more complications than using a clamp and crushing method. Other differences were seen in just one or two studies and weren't always consistent. 

For other things like needing blood transfusions or how long people stayed in the hospital, the studies didn't show much difference. Some studies suggested that using less pressure during surgery might help, but the evidence wasn't strong. 

There's not enough good information to say if using special equipment for liver surgery helps or hurts. The studies were small and the results weren't very precise. So, we don't know if using this equipment is better or worse than other methods. It's best to use it only in research settings right now.

output: This review looked at 14 studies that followed about 1.6 million women and their babies. Most studies found no link between using topical corticosteroids during pregnancy and problems like premature birth, low birth weight, or birth defects. Some studies suggested a slight increase in low birth weight for women who used stronger corticosteroids, but the evidence wasn't strong enough to be sure. Using weaker corticosteroids seemed to help prevent baby deaths. Overall, the evidence suggests that using any strength of topical corticosteroids during pregnancy doesn't seem to cause major problems. However, more research is needed to confirm these findings, especially around low birth weight and the effects of different strengths of corticosteroids.

This review looked at 62 studies with 4241 participants to see if oral morphine modified release (Mm/r) works better than regular morphine (MIR) for pain relief in people with cancer. Most of the studies didn't follow proper methods to make sure they were fair. 

The studies showed that Mm/r was as good as MIR for pain relief. Some studies found that Mm/r worked better for longer periods of time. But overall, the pain relief was similar between the two types of morphine. 

Most studies gave people different amounts of morphine to find out how much would work best for them. The amount varied from 25 mg to 2000 mg per day. People often had to try different doses to get enough pain relief. 

Some people couldn't take morphine because it made them feel sick or caused other problems. About 6% of people stopped taking it because of these side effects. 

While morphine is still a good option for pain, the studies weren't always done well. Many were small and were mainly done to show that different forms of morphine work equally well. 

Overall, morphine is still a very effective pain reliever, but more studies are needed to confirm its benefits and to look at how it compares to other pain medicines.
